title: Introduction to ethics
summary: A first-year survey of moral philosophy. Students learn to argue about ethics, test the major theories on hard cases, and apply them to global poverty, animals and artificial intelligence.
brief: Introduction to ethics for first-year university students: a 14-week semester, each week a 75-minute lecture and a 50-minute seminar. The textbook is James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, with primary readings each week. Week 1, what morality is (Rachels, chapter 1). Week 2, how to argue about ethics (Anthony Weston, A Rulebook for Arguments). Week 3, cultural relativism (Rachels, chapter 2). Week 4, utilitarianism (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, chapter 2; Rachels, chapters 7 and 8). Week 5, Kant (Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, section II; Rachels, chapters 9 and 10). Week 6, virtue ethics (Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, book II; Rachels, chapter 12). Week 7, social contract theory (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, chapters 13 to 15; Rachels, chapter 6). Week 8, the theories tested on hard cases (Judith Jarvis Thomson, "The Trolley Problem"). Weeks 9 and 10, what we owe distant strangers (Peter Singer, "Famine, Affluence, and Morality"; Thomas Nagel, "The Problem of Global Justice"). Week 11, the moral status of animals (Peter Singer, "All Animals Are Equal"; Carl Cohen, "The Case for the Use of Animals in Biomedical Research"). Week 12, who is responsible when an AI system causes harm (Andreas Matthias, "The responsibility gap"; Robert Sparrow, "Killer Robots"). Week 13, from a case to an argument: writing the final paper. Week 14, review for the exam. Students prepare the seminar discussion questions in advance. Grading: weekly reading responses 20%, seminar participation 10%, a 1,200-word paper defending one theory, due in week 7, 20%, a 2,000-word argumentative paper on one of the applied questions, due in week 13, 25%, and a final exam 25%, with rubrics for the papers.
policies:
Attendance at seminars is expected; participation is graded on preparation and contribution, not on how often you speak. Read the assigned texts before the seminar and bring them with you.

Papers are submitted through the course site by 11:59 p.m. on the due date. Late papers lose a third of a letter grade per day unless an extension is arranged before the due date.

AI tools may be used to brainstorm or check grammar, but not to write any part of submitted work; say in a note at the end of a paper how you used them. All work follows the university's academic integrity policy.

Students who need accommodations should contact Accessibility Services and let me know in the first two weeks.

l_ddfa785c31be.title: What morality is
l_ddfa785c31be.summary: Students ask what morality demands, using Rachels's minimum conception: reason, and equal consideration of everyone's interests.
readings: James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapter 1
suggestedReadings: Plato, Euthyphro
Mary Midgley, "Trying Out One's New Sword"

segments.title: Baby Theresa: what would you decide?
segments.description:
Briefly recall the case from the reading: Baby Theresa, born in Florida in 1992 with anencephaly, whose parents asked doctors to donate her organs to other infants. Explain that the proposed removal would occur while she was alive and cause her death; when she died, her organs had deteriorated too much to be transplanted.
Students vote by show of hands on whether the doctors should have taken the organs.
Three or four volunteers give the reason behind their vote, and the lecturer writes each reason on the board without comment.
segments.teacherNotes: The aim is to surface reasons, not settle the case. Expect ‘it feels wrong’ and ‘it saves lives’. Later, point out which answers are reasons and which are reactions. Take care: students may have personal experience of disability or infant loss.

segments.title: The minimum conception and what it leaves open
segments.description:
Present Rachels’s minimum conception with slides: morality is the effort to guide conduct by reason, while giving equal weight to everyone’s interests.
Unpack each half with chapter 1's cases: Theresa, Tracy Latimer in Saskatchewan in 1993, and the conjoined twins Jodie and Mary in Manchester in 2000. Return to the reasons on the board and sort them into good reasons and mere reactions.
Show that equal consideration is not identical treatment: a doctor treats the sickest patient first because that patient’s interest is greater. Note that impartiality counts your own interests too.
Close by noting that the definition does not say which reasons are best, and that the major theories offer rival answers later in the course.
segments.teacherNotes: Paraphrase Rachels and point students to the minimum conception section of chapter 1. Do not quote from memory. Common mistake: hearing ‘reason’ as ‘cold calculation’. Likely objection: ‘Whose reasons count?’ Answer: everyone’s interests count; assess the reasons by examining the relevant facts and arguments impartially. The definition is thin, not complete.

segments.title: Custom, law, self-interest or moral reason?
segments.description:
In pairs, students sort five short statements into custom, law, self-interest or moral reason, and note the reason for each choice.
Some statements fit more than one category, and students must say so.
The lecturer takes each in turn, asks one pair to defend its sorting, then asks the room whether anyone disagrees.
segments.teacherNotes:
Statements and expected answers:
1. Tipping 15 to 20 percent at US restaurants because everyone does: custom.
2. Stopping at a red light at 3 a.m. only because a camera records it: law, driven by self-interest.
3. Returning extra change a cashier gave you by mistake because she may have to cover the loss: moral reason.
4. Not cheating on an exam only because you fear expulsion: self-interest.
5. Hiding a person escaping slavery in 1850 despite the Fugitive Slave Act because returning them would deny their freedom and expose them to harm: moral reason against law.
Mistake: treating self-interest as never moral.

segments.title: Tracy Latimer under the two tests
segments.description:
In groups of three, students apply both tests to Robert Latimer’s killing of his daughter Tracy: what reasons were given, and whose interests were weighed?
Each group names one reason it finds strong and one it finds weak, and says why.
Groups report back in turn, and the lecturer records where they agree and disagree about how interests were counted.
segments.teacherNotes: Facts: Tracy was 12, with severe cerebral palsy; her father killed her in 1993 and was convicted of second-degree murder. Expect strong disagreement. Keep attention on reasons and impartiality, not on a verdict. Remind students to treat the people involved with respect.

segments.title: Preparing the seminar
segments.description:
Restate the two parts of the minimum conception in one sentence.
Remind students that the seminar is led by them, using the discussion questions they have prepared.
Ask them to bring one example where law or custom and morality came apart.
segments.teacherNotes: Seminar leaders should send their questions to the instructor beforehand. Preparation counts toward seminar participation, 10% of the grade.

segments.title: Is reason enough?
segments.description:
Two student leaders open with the question they prepared: which of chapter 1's cases was hardest, and what kind of reason did you rely on?
Students then close-read Rachels’s account of the minimum conception and test it. Can someone follow good reasons and still do wrong?
The leaders raise the friend-versus-stranger case: you can save only one of two drowning people. Students ask each other to point to the exact passage that supports a claim.
segments.teacherNotes: Instructor stays silent unless the discussion stalls; then ask who has a reason different from the last speaker’s. Likely positions: impartiality conflicts with loyalty to family and friends; reason alone is silent on what to value. Steer toward the definition being a minimum, not a full theory. No slides.

segments.title: Is legal the same as moral?
segments.description:
Students bring the example they were asked to prepare, where law or custom and morality came apart, and the leaders pick two for the group.
As a shared case they also consider the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which required citizens to help return people who had escaped slavery.
The group asks what reasons a person could give for obeying or defying a law, and whether those are moral reasons.
segments.teacherNotes: Draw out that law and custom give reasons to act (avoid punishment, belong to a group) but not necessarily moral reasons. Some will argue obeying law is itself moral; let others test that claim. Save custom as a topic for cultural relativism later in the course.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, what morality demands according to the minimum conception.
The leaders ask the group which statements captured both reason and impartiality, and which missed one.
The leaders summarize the strongest points and one unresolved question. The instructor points to the assigned sections of Anthony Weston’s A Rulebook for Arguments for next time and asks everyone to bring one example of a fallacy in a moral argument, from the reading or from public debate.
segments.teacherNotes: Good answers name both parts. Common gaps: reason with no mention of impartiality, or impartiality with no mention of everyone’s interests, including one’s own. Record the unresolved question and open next time with it. Remind students of the weekly reading response.

keyIdeas: Rachels’s minimum conception: morality is, at the very least, the effort to guide conduct by reason while giving equal weight to the interests of everyone affected.
A moral judgment needs good reasons. A feeling, a habit or an authority’s say-so does not count as one.
Impartiality means each person’s interests count the same, with no favorites. It does not mean everyone gets identical treatment.
Moral reasons are not the same as custom, law or self-interest. Each of these can agree with morality, and each can conflict with it.
The minimum conception is a starting point. It leaves open which reasons are best, and the major theories later in the course answer that.

vocabulary.definition: At the very least, the effort to guide conduct by reason while giving equal weight to the interests of everyone affected.
Rachels’s thin definition of morality, which holds that morality requires reason and impartiality and does not say what else it requires.
A consideration about what we ought to do that rests on the interests of those affected and can be checked impartially.
Treating each person’s interests as equally important, without favoritism.
What is good or bad for a being: its welfare, needs and preferences.
A practice a group follows by habit or tradition, which carries social approval but not necessarily moral force.
A rule enforced by a legal authority, which can be just or unjust.
Concern for one’s own benefit, which is a reason to act but not by itself a moral reason.

study.overview: This lesson asked what morality demands. Using Rachels’s minimum conception from chapter 1, we saw that morality is, at the very least, the effort to guide conduct by reason while giving equal weight to the interests of everyone affected. We then used that definition to separate moral reasons from custom, law and self-interest, and applied it to hard cases such as Baby Theresa and Tracy Latimer. The definition is a starting point. It does not tell you which reasons are best, and the major theories later in the course offer rival answers.

points.heading: The minimum conception: reason and equal consideration
points.explanation: Rachels’s minimum conception has two parts. First, morality is guided by reason: a moral judgment needs good reasons, and a feeling, a habit or an authority’s say-so does not count as one. Second, it gives equal weight to the interests of everyone affected. Take Baby Theresa, born in Florida in 1992 with anencephaly, whose parents asked doctors to donate her organs to other infants. ‘It saves lives’ points to the interests of the infants who could be helped, so it is a reason that can be examined. ‘It feels wrong’ reports a reaction. It may be worth explaining, but by itself it gives us nothing to weigh. Do not hear ‘reason’ as ‘cold calculation’. It means being able to say why, and to check the facts and arguments fairly. To revisit the definition, reread the minimum conception section of chapter 1 and paraphrase it in your own words.

points.heading: Impartiality is not identical treatment
points.explanation: Impartiality means each person’s interests count the same, with no favorites. It does not mean everyone gets the same treatment. A doctor who treats the sickest patient first is not showing favoritism. That patient’s interest in treatment is greater, so equal consideration of interests recommends treating that patient first. Impartiality also counts your own interests. They matter, but no more than anyone else’s. This is why the friend-versus-stranger case, where you can save only one of two drowning people, is a real test for the definition: it asks how far impartiality can sit alongside loyalty to friends and family.

points.heading: Moral reasons differ from custom, law and self-interest
points.explanation: Custom, law and self-interest all give people reasons to act, but they are not the same as moral reasons, and each can agree or conflict with morality. Tipping 15 to 20 percent at US restaurants because everyone does is custom. Stopping at a red light at 3 a.m. only because a camera records it is law, driven by self-interest. Not cheating on an exam only because you fear expulsion is self-interest. Returning extra change a cashier gave you by mistake, because she may have to cover the loss, is a moral reason: it concerns her interests. Self-interest is not always opposed to morality: it can line up with what morality asks. The test is whether the reason is about the interests of those affected. Law and morality can also come apart. In 1850 the Fugitive Slave Act required citizens to help return people who had escaped slavery. Someone who hid a fugitive because returning them would deny their freedom and expose them to harm acted on a moral reason against the law. Many cases fit more than one category, so say which reasons are at work and why.

points.heading: Applying both tests to Tracy Latimer, and what stays open
points.explanation: To use the two tests on a case, ask what reasons were given and whose interests were weighed. In 1993 Robert Latimer killed his daughter Tracy, who was 12 and had severe cerebral palsy. He was convicted of second-degree murder. Ask whether the reasons offered can be checked against the facts, and whether Tracy’s own interests counted equally with her family’s. Reasonable people disagree here, and the aim is to examine the reasoning, not to hand down a verdict. Notice what the definition does not do. It does not tell us which reasons are best, and it does not settle whether someone could follow good reasons and still do wrong. Chapter 1's other cases, such as the conjoined twins Jodie and Mary in Manchester in 2000, raise the same open questions. The minimum conception is thin, not complete. The major theories later in the course try to fill it in, and each gives a different answer.

l_d3ca41845cd9.title: How to argue about ethics
l_d3ca41845cd9.summary: Students learn to separate premises from conclusions, spot common fallacies, and give and answer objections fairly.
readings: Anthony Weston, A Rulebook for Arguments
suggestedReadings: Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument
Nigel Warburton, Thinking from A to Z

segments.title: From Baby Theresa to a claim and a reason
segments.description:
Recall Baby Theresa from last time. Pairs state in one sentence what they think the doctors should have done, then give the single best reason for it.
Take two pairs’ answers aloud and put them on the first slide as a claim with a reason beside it.
Ask the room which part is the claim and which is the reason.
segments.teacherNotes: Students will usually blend claim and reason into one sentence. That is the point: it motivates separating them. Accept either verdict; this is not a debate yet.

segments.title: Premises, conclusions and reconstruction
segments.description:
Define argument, premise and conclusion with slides. Show indicator words such as since, because, so and therefore.
Following Weston’s advice to distinguish premises from conclusion, reconstruct one possible argument from the Baby Theresa case in standard form on the slide.
Show how a hidden premise appears when the step from premises to conclusion feels too quick.
End on the question: does the conclusion follow, and are the premises true?
segments.teacherNotes: Model on slides: P1 Theresa will never be conscious. P2 What is never conscious has no interests. C Removing her organs would not harm her. Hidden premise: someone with no interests cannot be harmed. Add this as P3, then test the inference separately from the truth of the premises. Stress that reconstruction is not agreement.

segments.title: Reconstruct three arguments
segments.description:
In pairs, students rewrite each of three short arguments as numbered premises and a conclusion. They add any unstated premise they think the speaker needs.
Pairs compare with the next pair, then the lecturer takes one reconstruction per argument and tests it against the slide.
Note where pairs disagree about what the conclusion is.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers:
1. “Since lying betrays the trust of the person deceived, and betraying trust harms them, lying is wrong.” P1 Lying betrays trust. P2 Betraying trust harms the person. C Lying is wrong. Hidden: harming people is wrong.
2. “Capital punishment is wrong: it cannot be undone, and courts sometimes convict the innocent.” P1 Execution is irreversible. P2 Courts sometimes convict the innocent. C Capital punishment is wrong. Hidden: courts can convict innocent people of capital crimes; a punishment is wrong if it risks irreversibly punishing an innocent person. Identify the latter as a contestable moral premise.
3. “Theresa will never be conscious, so she has no interests. Something with no interests cannot be harmed. So taking her organs would not harm her.” P1 She will never be conscious. P2 No interests without consciousness. P3 No interests means no harm. C Taking her organs would not harm her.

segments.title: Three fallacies and fair objections
segments.description:
Present ad hominem, straw man and appeal to popularity, each with one moral example on a slide. Link appeal to popularity to the custom-versus-moral-reason distinction from last time.
Stress that a fallacy removes support for a conclusion but does not make the conclusion false.
Introduce the principle of charity and a three-step reply to an objection: restate it until its author agrees, grant what is true in it, then answer the strongest version.
Show a distorted and a fair restatement of an objection to the claim that Tracy Latimer’s father acted rightly.
segments.teacherNotes: Examples: ad hominem, “Ignore her case against vivisection; she is a vegan.” Straw man, turning “help the poor more” into “give away everything.” Popularity, “Everyone does it, so it is fine.” Students often think a fallacious argument has a false conclusion. Correct this each time.

segments.title: Name the move
segments.description:
Four short statements appear one at a time on the slide. Students decide individually what the move is, then vote by show of hands.
The lecturer asks one student per statement to defend the answer in a sentence.
The class corrects any answer that confuses a weak argument with a false conclusion.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. “Don’t listen to her case against the death penalty; she has never been a victim of crime.” Ad hominem.
2. A: “Rich countries should eat less meat.” B: “So you want to ban all farming.” Straw man.
3. “Most people in our town think the policy is fine, so it is morally fine.” Appeal to popularity.
4. “Torture is wrong because it inflicts severe suffering on someone who cannot defend themselves.” No fallacy; a premise-based argument (control item).

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: Weston’s rules under pressure
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared: which of Weston’s rules is hardest to follow when you feel strongly about the topic, and why?
Students answer with a specific passage from A Rulebook for Arguments.
The leaders then pick two of the fallacy examples classmates found and prepared. The group names the fallacy and asks whether the conclusion could still be true.
The instructor intervenes only to keep talk on the text.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely answers: avoiding loaded language, or starting from reliable premises. Push students to cite the page. If an example is not a fallacy at all, use it: ask what premise is missing. Instructor exposition stays under two minutes.

segments.title: Restate, then reply: the Latimer objection
segments.description:
In groups of three, one student defends the claim that Robert Latimer was right to end Tracy’s life because she was in constant pain. A second states an objection. The third restates the objection until the objector says it is fair.
The defender then replies to the restated objection only. Roles rotate twice.
Groups report back on where the restatement was hardest to get right.
segments.teacherNotes: Sample fair objection: Tracy’s life had value to her, and others may not judge that a disabled life is not worth living. Distortion to watch for: “So you think disabled people should suffer.” Circulate; correct restatements that add or drop claims.

segments.title: What a fair objection requires
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, what makes an objection fair to the position it targets.
The leaders ask the group for the one rule from today they will apply to their next paper.
The instructor names the reading to prepare next time.
segments.teacherNotes: Good answers: the person whose position is challenged would accept the objection’s representation of that position; the objection targets the strongest version; it attacks a premise or the link, not the person. Tie to the paper defending one theory, where objections must be answered fairly.

keyIdeas: An argument gives reasons (premises) for a claim (the conclusion). Reconstructing it means writing both out plainly, including any premise the speaker left unstated.
A moral view is only as strong as its premises and the link from premises to conclusion. Weston’s rules are tools for testing both.
Three fallacies recur in moral debate: ad hominem, straw man and appeal to popularity. Each replaces a reason with something that only looks like one.
Spotting a fallacy shows that one argument fails. It does not show that the conclusion is false.
To answer an objection fairly, restate it so its author would accept your version, and only then reply.

vocabulary.definition: A set of statements in which some (the premises) are offered as reasons for another (the conclusion).
A statement given as a reason to accept a conclusion.
The claim an argument tries to establish.
A pattern of reasoning that looks like support for a conclusion but gives none.
Attacking the person who makes a claim instead of the reasons offered for it.
Answering a distorted or weaker version of someone’s view rather than the view they hold.
Treating the fact that many people believe or do something as a reason that it is right or true.
Interpreting an opponent’s argument in its strongest reasonable form before replying.

Straw man: “help the poor more” becomes “give away everything”
Popularity: “Everyone does it, so it is fine.”
Each swaps a reason for something that only looks like one
slides.notes: Present each fallacy with its moral example. Link appeal to popularity to the distinction between custom and moral reason from last time: a practice being common does not show it is right. Stress that a fallacy removes support for a conclusion but does not make the conclusion false. Students often think a fallacious argument has a false conclusion. Correct this each time it comes up.

slides.title: Answering an objection fairly
bullets: Principle of charity: take the strongest version
1. Restate it until its author agrees
2. Grant what is true in it
3. Answer the strongest version
slides.notes: Illustrate with an objection to the claim that Tracy Latimer’s father acted rightly. A fair restatement: Tracy’s life had value to her, and others may not judge that a disabled life is not worth living. A distorted restatement: “So you think disabled people should suffer.” Ask what the distortion adds that the objector never said. In the seminar, students practice restating an objection until its author accepts it, then replying only to that restated version.

slides.title: Name the move
bullets: 1. “Don’t listen to her case against the death penalty; she has never been a victim of crime.”
2. A: “Rich countries should eat less meat.” B: “So you want to ban all farming.”
3. “Most people in our town think the policy is fine, so it is morally fine.”
4. “Torture is wrong because it inflicts severe suffering on someone who cannot defend themselves.”
slides.notes: Reveal the statements one at a time. Students decide individually what the move is, then vote by show of hands. Ask one student per statement to defend the answer in a sentence. Answers: 1 ad hominem; 2 straw man; 3 appeal to popularity; 4 no fallacy, a premise-based argument and the control item. Correct any answer that confuses a weak argument with a false conclusion.

study.overview: This lesson gave you a method for arguing about ethics. First you reconstruct an argument: write its premises and conclusion out plainly, including any premise the speaker left unstated. Then you test it, asking whether the premises are true and whether the conclusion follows. You also met three fallacies (ad hominem, straw man and appeal to popularity) and a way to answer objections fairly. Weston’s A Rulebook for Arguments supplies the tools. Use this guide to revisit the examples from class and to prepare for your next paper.

points.heading: Reconstruct an argument before you judge it
points.explanation:
An argument gives reasons (premises) for a claim (the conclusion). Indicator words such as since, because, so and therefore often mark the reasons and the claim. Reconstruction means writing both out as numbered premises and a conclusion. Add any premise the speaker left unstated, which usually shows up when the step from premises to conclusion feels too quick.

Example from the Baby Theresa case:
P1 Theresa will never be conscious.
P2 What is never conscious has no interests.
P3 Someone with no interests cannot be harmed (the hidden premise).
C Removing her organs would not harm her.

Once the argument is on the page, test two things separately: are the premises true, and does the conclusion follow from them? Here P3 is the premise most worth challenging. Reconstructing an argument is not agreeing with it. It only makes the argument clear enough to test. Take the claim ‘Capital punishment is wrong: it cannot be undone, and courts sometimes convict the innocent.’ It also needs a hidden premise: a punishment is wrong if it risks irreversibly punishing an innocent person. That premise is a contestable moral claim, so name it and defend or challenge it openly.

points.heading: Three fallacies replace a reason with something that only looks like one
points.explanation:
Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument: ‘Ignore her case against vivisection; she is a vegan.’ Her way of life tells us nothing about whether her premises are true.

A straw man distorts a position and then attacks the distortion. If A says ‘Rich countries should eat less meat’ and B replies ‘So you want to ban all farming,’ B has answered a claim A never made. Likewise, turning ‘help the poor more’ into ‘give away everything’ misrepresents the view.

Appeal to popularity treats agreement as proof: ‘Most people in our town think the policy is fine, so it is morally fine.’ This echoes the difference between custom and moral reason from last time. What many people accept is a fact about custom. It is not by itself a reason that the policy is right.

Not every argument is fallacious. ‘Torture is wrong because it inflicts severe suffering on someone who cannot defend themselves’ gives a reason, a premise about suffering and helplessness, that can be examined on its merits. When you suspect a fallacy, ask what reason is missing or being replaced.

points.heading: A fallacy sinks the argument, not the conclusion
points.explanation:
A common mistake is to think that spotting a fallacy shows the conclusion is false. It does not. It shows only that this argument gives no support for the conclusion. The conclusion might still be true, and another argument might support it.

Suppose someone argues that the death penalty is wrong and is told, ‘Don’t listen to her; she has never been a victim of crime.’ That is ad hominem, so the reply fails. But the claim that the death penalty is wrong has not been refuted. It simply has not yet been answered. The same holds for your own side: if you catch an opponent in a fallacy, you have not won the point. You have only cleared away one bad argument, and the question of whether the conclusion is true remains open.

points.heading: Answer an objection fairly: restate, grant, then reply
points.explanation:
The principle of charity asks you to engage the strongest version of a view. In practice, follow three steps. First, restate the objection until its author agrees you have it right. Second, grant what is true in it. Third, answer the strongest version.

Consider the claim that Robert Latimer was right to end his daughter Tracy’s life because she was in constant pain. A fair objection is: Tracy’s life had value to her, and others may not judge that a disabled life is not worth living. A distorted version is: ‘So you think disabled people should suffer.’ The distortion adds a claim the objector never made, which makes it a straw man.

A fair objection is one the challenged person would accept as an accurate account of their position. It targets the strongest version of that position. It attacks a premise or the link from premises to conclusion, not the person. When you write your paper defending one theory, apply this standard to every objection you answer.

l_8248014df748.title: Cultural relativism
l_8248014df748.summary: Students test the claim that right and wrong depend on culture, using the cultural differences argument and its consequences.
readings: James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapter 2
suggestedReadings: Ruth Benedict, "Anthropology and the Abnormal"
Herodotus, Histories, book 3

segments.title: The Greeks and the Callatians
segments.description:
Tell Herodotus’s story from Rachels, chapter 2. Darius asked the Greeks, who burn their dead, what it would take for them to eat their dead fathers. He then asked the Callatians, who eat their dead, whether they would burn them.
Each student decides alone which practice, if either, seems wrong, and writes down the reason. Pairs compare reasons and say whether each reason is a moral reason or a custom, using last time’s distinction.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect most to call eating the dead wrong because it feels disgusting. Press: is disgust a moral reason or a custom? Keep this short; it sets up the argument that follows. Some students may find the topic uncomfortable; stay matter-of-fact.

segments.title: Reconstructing the cultural differences argument
segments.description:
Present on slides the argument in numbered form. Premise 1: different cultures have different moral codes. Conclusion: there is no objective truth in morality; right and wrong are only matters of opinion that vary from culture to culture.
Use the Greeks and Callatians and the historical accounts of Inuit infanticide that Rachels discusses, which he explains partly through severe resource scarcity, as the evidence for premise 1. Ask what unstated premise links the two steps. Explain that adding this premise makes the inference valid, but the added premise needs justification; the original argument from disagreement alone remains invalid.
Then show why the argument is invalid: it moves from what people believe to what is the case. Societies once disagreed about the shape of the Earth, and there is still a fact about it.
segments.teacherNotes: Unstated premise: if cultures disagree about a matter, there is no objective truth about it. Rachels notes the Inuit still value children; the difference lies in circumstances. Common mistake: concluding that relativism is false because the argument is invalid. Recall last time: a failed argument does not make the conclusion false.

segments.title: Does it follow?
segments.description:
In pairs, students read five arguments on the slide. For each, they decide whether the conclusion follows from the premise, and give a reason.
They then identify which arguments move from differing beliefs to the absence of truth, and explain how item 3 applies that move to morality.
Go through the answers as a group and record which arguments pairs found hardest.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers:
1. Some societies once taught that the Earth is flat, so there is no truth about its shape. Does not follow: belief differs, the fact does not.
2. Doctors disagree about a diagnosis, so there is no fact about what the patient has. Does not follow.
3. Cultures differ over how to treat the dead, so there is no objective truth about how to treat the dead. Does not follow; same form as the cultural differences argument.
4. Cultures differ over how to treat the dead, so what is right in a given culture depends on what that culture’s code says. Does not follow from the difference alone; it needs the relativist premise.
5. Societies disagree about slavery, so we cannot be sure slavery is wrong. Does not follow: how sure we can be depends on the reasons on each side, not on the bare fact of disagreement.

segments.title: Consequences of relativism and what we can still learn
segments.description:
Present on slides what relativism implies, stated conditionally. Where a society’s accepted code endorses persecution of a group, relativism says the persecution is right there. Where reformers challenge that code, relativism says they are wrong.
Add that societies are seldom of one mind. Many people inside a society may reject its dominant code, and relativism has no way to count them as right.
Then present Rachels’s two lessons: our customs may reflect cultural prejudice, and we should keep an open mind. Connect these with his separate argument that societies share some values, such as care for the young and prohibitions on murder.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress the conditional wording: the claim is about what the theory implies, not that any whole society agreed. Many Germans did not accept Nazi persecution, and antebellum US views on slavery were divided. Relativism says dissenters are wrong by their society’s code, which is the problem. Shared values: Rachels argues societies could not survive without them.

segments.title: Does relativism imply it?
segments.description:
Four statements appear one at a time on the slide. Students decide alone whether each follows from cultural relativism, then vote by show of hands.
Ask one student who voted with the minority to give the reason. For the seminar, each student prepares one example of a practice that differs across cultures, keeping what is documented separate from their own interpretation. The two student leaders prepare an opening question on whether relativism supports tolerance.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers:
1. Where the accepted code endorses persecution of a minority, the persecution is right there. Follows.
2. A reformer who challenges her own society’s accepted code is mistaken by that code. Follows.
3. Our own society’s code is the best one. Does not follow: relativism denies it any special status.
4. Another society’s moral code cannot be judged inferior by an objective, culture-independent standard. Follows. This does not establish a universal duty to tolerate other societies’ practices.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: does relativism support tolerance?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared: does cultural relativism give us a reason to be tolerant of other cultures, or does it undermine tolerance?
The group follows the leaders’ thread, citing chapter 2. The instructor speaks only to keep the discussion on the text.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely directions: relativists often urge tolerance, but if tolerance is only one society’s code, an intolerant society is right by its own code. Tolerance cannot be binding on everyone. Pointers: Rachels’s claim 6 (judging others is arrogant) and the shared-values lesson. Do not give a verdict; let students reach it.

segments.title: Real difference or shared value?
segments.description:
Students bring the example they were asked to prepare: a practice that differs across cultures, and the beliefs and values beneath it. The leaders pick two for the group.
For each, the group asks whether the difference lies in values or in beliefs and circumstances, as with the Inuit. They then ask what relativism and its critics would each say.
segments.teacherNotes: Fallback if few examples are offered: the Greeks and Callatians. Ask whether both groups might be honoring their dead in different ways. Rachels offers this interpretation of the Callatians as a possibility, not a documented explanation of their beliefs. Examples may touch students’ own cultures: invite volunteers, never ask a student to speak for a culture, and keep the focus on the practice, not on people.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, whether the cultural differences argument works and why.
The instructor then names one question left open for next time.
segments.teacherNotes: Good one-sentence answers say the argument is invalid because disagreement does not show there is no truth. Weak answers say only that relativism is wrong or that everyone has a right to an opinion. Open question: if relativism fails, which account of right and wrong replaces it?

keyIdeas: Cultural relativism holds that a society’s moral code determines what is right within that society, and that no code is better than another. Rachels breaks the view into separate claims so each can be tested.

The cultural differences argument reconstructs as two steps: premise 1 says different cultures have different moral codes. The conclusion says there is no objective truth in morality, only opinion that varies by culture.

The argument is invalid. Disagreement about a question does not show that the question has no answer. Societies once disagreed about the shape of the Earth, yet there is a fact of the matter. As last time, showing that this argument fails does not show that relativism is false.

Stated conditionally, relativism implies that persecution is right wherever the accepted code endorses it, and that reformers are wrong wherever they challenge the accepted code. Societies are rarely of one mind, so these are implications of the theory, not descriptions of any one society.

Relativism still teaches three things: our own customs may be cultural prejudice, we should keep an open mind, and some differences in practice rest on shared values applied in different circumstances.

vocabulary.definition: The view that a society’s moral code determines what is right within that society, and that no code is better than another.
The argument that because cultures have different moral codes, there is no objective truth in morality.
The set of moral rules and standards accepted in a society.
A truth that holds whatever any person or society happens to believe.
An argument is valid when its conclusion follows from its premises. If the premises could be true while the conclusion is false, it is invalid.
Change in a society’s moral views that is an improvement, not just a difference.
Moral commitments found in every society, such as caring for the young and a ban on murder.

study.overview: Cultural relativism says that a society’s moral code determines what is right within that society, and that no code is better than another. Rachels, in chapter 2, breaks the view into separate claims so each can be tested. In this lesson we reconstructed the cultural differences argument, showed why it is invalid, and then asked what relativism implies and what it still teaches. The central lesson is that showing an argument fails is not the same as showing its conclusion false. Use this guide to review the argument, the consequences, and the lessons that survive.

points.heading: The cultural differences argument and why it is invalid
points.explanation: The argument has two steps. Premise 1: different cultures have different moral codes. Conclusion: there is no objective truth in morality; right and wrong are only opinions that vary from culture to culture. Evidence for premise 1 came from Herodotus’s story of the Greeks, who burn their dead, and the Callatians, who eat theirs, and from the historical accounts of Inuit infanticide that Rachels discusses. The inference is invalid because it moves from what people believe to what is the case. Disagreement about a question does not show that the question has no answer. Societies once disagreed about the shape of the Earth, yet there is a fact about it. The same form of reasoning would show that doctors who disagree about a diagnosis have no fact to find. The argument can be made valid by adding an unstated premise: if cultures disagree about a matter, there is no objective truth about it. But that premise needs its own justification, and the original argument from disagreement alone remains invalid. A common mistake is to conclude that relativism is false because this argument fails. As we saw last time, a failed argument does not make its conclusion false. It only means this argument gives us no reason to accept it.

points.heading: What relativism implies
points.explanation: Stated conditionally, relativism implies that persecution of a group is right wherever the accepted code endorses it, and that reformers are wrong wherever they challenge the accepted code. These are claims about what the theory implies, not descriptions of any one society that agreed to them. Societies are rarely of one mind. Many Germans did not accept Nazi persecution, and views on slavery in the antebellum United States were divided. Relativism says dissenters are wrong by their society’s code, and it has no way to count them as right. That is the problem. Relativism also gives our own society’s code no special status, so it does not follow from the theory that our code is the best one. It does follow that another society’s code cannot be judged inferior by an objective, culture-independent standard. This does not establish a universal duty to tolerate other societies’ practices. In seminar we asked whether relativism supports tolerance. If tolerance is only one society’s code, then an intolerant society is right by its own code, so tolerance cannot bind everyone.

points.heading: What relativism still teaches
points.explanation: Even if relativism fails, Rachels draws two lessons from it. First, our own customs may be cultural prejudice rather than moral truth. Second, we should keep an open mind when we meet unfamiliar practices. His discussion of disagreement adds a third point: some differences in practice rest on shared values applied in different circumstances. The Inuit case shows this: Rachels notes that the Inuit still value children, and the difference lies in circumstances, including severe resource scarcity. Rachels also argues that societies share some values, such as care for the young and prohibitions on murder, because societies could not survive without them. When you analyze a practice, ask whether the difference lies in values or in beliefs and circumstances. Keep what is documented separate from your own interpretation. For example, Rachels offers the idea that the Greeks and Callatians might both be honoring their dead in different ways, but he offers it as a possibility, not as a documented account of what the Callatians believed. The open question for next time: if relativism fails, which account of right and wrong replaces it?

l_8c26f19c9165.title: Utilitarianism
l_8c26f19c9165.summary: Students examine Mill's claim that right acts maximize happiness, and weigh the standard objections to it.
readings: James Rachels and Stuart Rachels, The Elements of Moral Philosophy, chapters 7 and 8
suggestedReadings: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
J. J. C. Smart and Bernard Williams, Utilitarianism: For and Against

segments.title: What would a happiness-counter count? Tracy Latimer
segments.description:
Recall Robert Latimer and his daughter Tracy from earlier in the course.
In pairs, students list whose happiness and suffering would have to be counted if one asked only which outcome produces the most happiness.
Take two lists from the room and note where they differ.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect pairs to list Tracy, her parents, her siblings and disabled people generally. The last group is a hard one: it raises how a person’s life is valued. Do not settle the verdict. This only motivates the principle presented next.

segments.title: Mill’s greatest happiness principle
segments.description:
Present on slides the principle as Mill states it in chapter 2: actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse.
Define happiness as pleasure and the absence of pain, and show the equal-counting clause: the agent’s own happiness counts no more than a stranger’s.
Use a hypothetical application to model a numbered argument: premise 1, an act is right if it maximizes overall happiness; premise 2, suppose keeping a particular promise maximizes overall happiness; conclusion, keeping that promise is right. Link equal counting to impartiality in the minimum conception.
Define consequentialism and contrast it with judging an act by motive.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: hearing ‘happiness’ as the agent’s own. Mill counts everyone alike. Distinguish the standard of right, which is consequences, from the motive for acting, which Mill says does not decide whether the act is right. Point to Rachels, chapter 7, for Bentham’s version.

segments.title: Higher and lower pleasures
segments.description:
Present on slides the charge that a theory built on pleasure is a doctrine fit only for pigs, and Mill’s reply in chapter 2.
Explain the competent-judge test: if people who have experienced two pleasures prefer one, even when it comes with more discontent, that one is higher.
Set out the contrast Mill draws between a dissatisfied human and a satisfied pig, and between a dissatisfied Socrates and a satisfied fool.
Pose the problem for the seminar: does this test bring in a standard other than pleasure?
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: reading ‘higher’ as ‘more intense’. Mill ranks by quality, and the judges’ preference is the evidence. Another: saying Mill thinks the pig is better off. He does not. Flag that the critics’ worry returns in the seminar.

segments.title: Objections from justice and promises, and Mill’s replies
segments.description:
Present the two objections from Rachels, chapter 8: some acts maximize happiness yet seem unjust, and some seem owed because of what was promised, not because of what follows.
Groups of three take Case A, then Case B. Each group says what the principle seems to require, why that seems wrong, and whether the reply from long-run consequences and secondary principles answers it.
Bring the room together on whether the reply holds once the case is stipulated so that the injustice or the broken promise is never discovered.
segments.teacherNotes:
Case A: Suppose a sheriff can stop a riot that would kill several people only by framing and executing an innocent man. Stipulate that, after all immediate and long-run harms and benefits are counted, framing him produces more overall happiness than any available alternative. Expected: the principle seems to favor framing; long-run loss of trust is Mill’s reply; the objector stipulates secrecy.
Case B: You promised a dying friend to give her savings to her chess club, but a hospital would gain slightly more happiness. Expected: backward-looking reason; reply is that promise-breaking erodes trust; the objector stipulates secrecy.
Both cases are hypothetical. Mill’s secondary principles are rules of thumb, not extra moral standards.

segments.title: The demandingness objection
segments.description:
Present Case C on a slide, then name the demandingness objection: if each person’s happiness counts equally, the principle seems to require giving up almost everything.
In groups of three, one student reconstructs the objection as premises and a conclusion, a second restates it until the first accepts the restatement as fair, and the third tests each reply offered by the groups.
Discuss whether long-run effects on Dana’s health, dependents and earning capacity limit the required sacrifice, and whether the remaining demand is still excessive. Explain why the standard-versus-motive distinction does not answer an objection about how much sacrifice is required.
Name what a reply to this objection would have to do: accept the demand, limit it, or deny that it counts against the theory.
segments.teacherNotes: Case C: Dana earns a comfortable salary and spends part of it on concert tickets, restaurant meals and a new phone. Each such dollar would do more good if given to famine relief. Expected: the principle seems to require redirecting the listed discretionary spending to relief. To argue for further giving, students must add the premise that further donations continue to produce greater overall benefits than costs, including effects on Dana and anyone dependent on Dana. The standard-versus-motive distinction concerns motives, not extent of sacrifice. Singer defends demanding duties of aid later in the course.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: is the competent-judge test still pleasure?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared: if higher pleasures are those competent judges prefer, does Mill still hold that happiness alone is what matters?
Students answer by returning to Mill’s chapter 2 and to Rachels, chapters 7 and 8. Leaders ask them to say which reading of ‘preferred’ they are using.
The instructor intervenes only to ask for a premise stated plainly or a source for a claim.
segments.teacherNotes: Two readings help: competent judges’ preference identifies a pleasure as better in quality, or it reflects a value other than pleasure. The first preserves Mill’s claim that pleasure alone has intrinsic value but must explain qualitative superiority. The second challenges that claim. Press students to explain which reading chapter 2 supports.

segments.title: Which objection is strongest, and does the reply work?
segments.description:
Students bring the objection they were asked to prepare: one objection to utilitarianism from Rachels, chapter 8, or from the lecture, with the best reply to it and the reason they accept or reject that reply.
The leaders pick two for the group. Each presenter restates the objection until the group agrees it is fair, then gives the reply.
The group tests whether the reply answers that objection or a different one.
segments.teacherNotes: These preparations also serve seminar participation. Watch for replies that answer a nearby objection, for example using the standard-versus-motive distinction against demandingness. If the leaders pick two on the same objection, ask for a third on a different one.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, which objection to utilitarianism they find strongest and why.
The leaders note which objections drew the most votes and where the room split.
The instructor names next time’s question: what a theory might say when consequences are not what counts.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept any objection if the student names it and gives a reason. Push gently if the reason merely states a feeling, as in the earlier work on reasons. Do not collect writing.

keyIdeas: Mill’s greatest happiness principle: actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce its opposite. Happiness means pleasure and the absence of pain, and everyone’s happiness counts equally.

Utilitarianism is a consequentialist theory. An act is judged by its results, not by the agent’s motive or by whether it keeps a rule. Mill’s distinction between standard and motive says what makes an act right, not what should drive the agent.

Mill separates pleasures by quality as well as quantity. A pleasure is higher if competent judges who have experienced both prefer it, even when the lower pleasure is more intense. His critics ask whether this appeals to something other than pleasure.

The standard objections target different features of the theory. The justice and rights objection and the promises objection say some acts are wrong even when they maximize happiness. Mill replies with long-run consequences and secondary principles. The demandingness objection says the principle requires too much sacrifice, and that needs a different reply.
Evaluating an objection means reconstructing it as premises and a conclusion, restating it so its author would accept it, and then testing whether the reply answers that objection or a different one.

Mill’s distinction by quality: a pleasure is higher if competent judges prefer it to another, even when the other is more intense.
A person who has experienced both of two pleasures and so can say which is preferable.
Rules of thumb, such as keeping promises, that summarize the long-run effects of kinds of acts.
The objection that equal counting of everyone’s happiness requires excessive personal sacrifice.
A justified claim to certain treatment or protection. The rights objection asks whether maximizing overall happiness can justify violating such a claim.

study.overview: This guide reviews what you did in the lecture and seminar on utilitarianism. Mill’s greatest happiness principle says an act is right if it tends to promote happiness and wrong if it tends to produce the opposite, and everyone’s happiness counts equally. You also saw Mill separate pleasures by quality, and you tested several standard objections. The aim is to evaluate an objection: reconstruct it, restate it fairly, and check that the reply answers that objection and not a nearby one.

points.heading: The greatest happiness principle and consequentialism
points.explanation: Mill states in chapter 2 that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse. Happiness means pleasure and the absence of pain. The equal-counting clause matters: your own happiness counts no more than a stranger’s. This is why ‘happiness’ does not mean the agent’s own, and why the clause links to impartiality. Utilitarianism is consequentialist: an act is judged by its results, not by the agent’s motive or by whether it keeps a rule. Mill’s distinction between standard and motive says what makes an act right (its consequences). It does not say what should drive the agent. A numbered argument shows the structure. Premise 1: an act is right if it maximizes overall happiness. Premise 2: suppose keeping a particular promise maximizes overall happiness. Conclusion: keeping that promise is right. Rachels, chapter 7, covers Bentham’s version for comparison.

points.heading: Higher and lower pleasures
points.explanation: Critics charge that a theory built on pleasure is a doctrine fit only for pigs. Mill replies that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity. His competent-judge test says that if people who have experienced two pleasures prefer one, even when it comes with more discontent, that pleasure is higher. ‘Higher’ does not mean ‘more intense’: Mill ranks by quality, and the judges’ preference is the evidence. His contrasts are a dissatisfied human against a satisfied pig, and a dissatisfied Socrates against a satisfied fool. Mill holds that the human and Socrates are better off, not the pig or the fool. The seminar question was whether this test brings in a standard other than pleasure. There are two readings of ‘preferred’. On the first, the preference identifies a pleasure as better in quality, which keeps Mill’s claim that pleasure alone has intrinsic value but leaves him to explain what qualitative superiority is. On the second, the preference reflects a value other than pleasure, which challenges that claim. Decide which reading chapter 2 supports, and cite the text.

points.heading: Objections from justice and promises, and Mill’s replies
points.explanation: Rachels, chapter 8, presents two objections. The justice and rights objection says some acts maximize happiness yet seem unjust. The promises objection says some acts are owed because of what was promised, not because of what follows. Consider two hypothetical cases. Case A: a sheriff can stop a riot that would kill several people only by framing and executing an innocent man. Suppose that, after all immediate and long-run harms and benefits are counted, framing him produces more overall happiness than any alternative. Case B: you promised a dying friend to give her savings to her chess club, but a hospital would gain slightly more happiness. Mill replies with long-run consequences and secondary principles: injustice and promise-breaking erode trust, and rules such as ‘keep promises’ are rules of thumb, not extra moral standards. The objector’s response is to stipulate that the injustice or broken promise is never discovered. Then the long-run loss of trust disappears, and the question is whether the reply still holds.

points.heading: The demandingness objection and how to evaluate objections
points.explanation: Case C: Dana earns a comfortable salary and spends part of it on concert tickets, restaurant meals and a new phone. Each such dollar would do more good if given to famine relief. The demandingness objection says that if each person’s happiness counts equally, the principle seems to require giving up almost everything. Reconstructed, it runs: the principle requires Dana to redirect the discretionary spending to relief, and to keep giving while giving does more good than harm; a correct moral theory would not demand that much sacrifice; so the principle is mistaken. To argue for further giving, you must add the premise that further donations keep producing greater overall benefits than costs, including effects on Dana and Dana’s dependents. Long-run effects on Dana’s health, dependents and earning capacity may limit the demand, and you can ask whether what remains is still excessive. The standard-versus-motive distinction does not answer this objection, because it concerns motives, not how much sacrifice is required. A reply must accept the demand, limit it, or deny that it counts against the theory. Singer defends demanding duties of aid later in the course. To evaluate any objection: reconstruct it as premises and a conclusion, restate it so its author would accept it, then test whether the reply answers that objection or a different one. Using the standard-versus-motive distinction against demandingness is a typical mismatch. Long-run consequences can limit the demand but do not remove it.

readings: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, sections I and II

segments.title: A promise that no one would miss
segments.description:
Recall the promises objection to utilitarianism from last time.
Pose a hypothetical. You borrow ten dollars from a wealthy friend and promise to repay it. She would never miss it, and you could do more good with it elsewhere.
In pairs, students decide whether Mill’s reply about long-run consequences and secondary principles fully explains why keeping the promise is a duty. Take two views from the room.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: the reply says promise-breaking weakens trust over time. Some students will say that is not why it feels wrong. Name that unease as the motive for today: Kant locates the wrong in the act, not its results.

segments.title: Duty, imperatives and the universal law formulation
segments.description:
Present on slides Kant’s claim in section I that moral worth lies in acting from duty, which reason recognizes, not from inclination. Contrast a shopkeeper who gives correct change because honesty is good for business with one who does so from duty.
Define hypothetical and categorical imperatives: if you want a good grade, study; do not make false promises, whatever you want.
Present the formulation: act only on a maxim you can will to be a universal law. Teach three steps: state the maxim as action plus purpose, imagine everyone acting on it, ask whether that is conceivable and whether you could will it.
Work the false promise: I will make a promise I do not intend to keep, in order to get a loan. Universal false promising destroys the practice of promising, so the purpose fails. Call this a contradiction in conception. Contrast it with refusing all help: universal nonassistance is conceivable, but a rational agent cannot consistently will it while willing the help they may need to pursue their ends. Call this a contradiction in will.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistakes: thinking Kant calls feelings bad (he says acting merely from inclination does not give an act moral worth; feelings may accompany acting from duty); treating the test as utilitarian, asking what would happen if everyone did it. Kant asks whether the maxim is coherent. The purpose belongs inside the maxim.

segments.title: Testing maxims against the universal law
segments.description:
In pairs, students receive four fully stated maxims, each with action and purpose, on a slide.
For each, they apply the three steps and decide whether the maxim passes. When it fails, they name the kind of contradiction.
Go through the answers together and take disagreements.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. I will make a promise I do not intend to keep, in order to get a loan I could not otherwise get. Fails: contradiction in conception.
2. I will cheat on an exam when sure not to be caught, in order to get a higher grade. Disputed item. The usual answer is a contradiction in conception: if everyone cheated whenever they could, a grade would no longer be taken as a sign of what a student knows, so the higher grade would lose the value that is the purpose of cheating. Some will reply that the mark still rises. Let them argue it; this maxim returns in the seminar as a test of how maxims are worded.
3. I will refuse help to anyone in need, in order to keep all my resources for myself. Fails: contradiction in will, because a rational agent wills the means needed to pursue their ends, yet this universal law rules out assistance they may need.
4. I will give money each month to a charity, in order to help people in need. Passes.
If students drop the purpose, return them to it.

segments.title: The humanity formulation
segments.description:
Present on slides the formulation: treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means.
Explain dignity as the worth persons have as rational agents. It has no price and cannot be traded against benefits.
Distinguish using someone from using them merely. Ask whether the person can share the aim and consent to how they are treated: a barista freely agreeing to serve a customer can consent, while a lender deceived by a false promise cannot consent to the actual arrangement. Explain that treating humanity as an end also requires supporting others’ permissible ends where possible and developing our own capacities.
Students then, in pairs, explain why the false-promise maxim fails the humanity formulation as well. Take two answers.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistake: treating someone as a means is always wrong. Kant forbids only merely as a means. Link to Rachels, chapter 10, on respect for persons. Kant takes the two formulations to give the same verdicts; students may doubt this.

segments.title: Two tests and the seminar questions
segments.description:
Summarize what each formulation asks of an act.
Remind students to bring Rachels, chapters 9 and 10, and section II of the Groundwork to the seminar, with the passage they have marked on the humanity formulation.
Remind the two student leaders to bring their prepared discussion questions.
Preview the Latimer case, which the seminar will approach through both Kant and Mill.
segments.teacherNotes: Seminar participation is graded at 10%. A Kantian view is a candidate theory for the paper defending one theory, graded at 20%. Suggest students note which formulation they find stronger.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: does the universal law test get it right?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared. Does the universal law test condemn exactly the acts we think wrong, or can a maxim be worded to pass or fail?
Students respond to each other, using maxims from the lecture and the objections in Rachels, chapter 9.
The leaders then pick one marked passage on the humanity formulation, and the group reconstructs Kant’s argument from it in numbered premises and a conclusion.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely points: a maxim can be worded too narrowly or broadly; Rachels, chapter 9, discusses conflicts between rules. Premise to find: rational agents are ends in themselves, so may not be used merely as means. Ask for page references; do not give answers.

segments.title: Latimer again: Kant or Mill?
segments.description:
The group returns to Robert Latimer and his daughter Tracy. Students first give the Kantian analysis in two parts: the maxim Latimer acted on, tested under the universal law formulation, and the humanity formulation.
Next they give the utilitarian answer as a conditional. They list what they would need to know before Mill’s principle gives a verdict.
Finally they ask whether grounding dignity in rational agency adequately protects people with profound cognitive disabilities. They treat this as a question of principle, not a judgment of Tracy’s capacities.
segments.teacherNotes: Missing information for the utilitarian: future experiences, alternatives such as better pain care, effects on family, indirect effects on disabled people and trust in carers. Kantians may disagree on the maxim. Redirect claims about Tracy’s capacities: not in the sources. Options on dignity: capacity, species membership, duties regarding all humans.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, whether the universal law or the humanity formulation seems more persuasive and why.
The leaders note which objections to Kant came up most.
The instructor names the question to carry forward: what a theory should say when it cannot give a determinate answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept any position with a reason. Ask students to tie the answer to a passage in the reading. These notes also help with the weekly reading responses.

keyIdeas: Kant holds that morality rests on reason, not on feeling or consequences. Only a good will, which acts from duty, is good without qualification.
A hypothetical imperative commands what to do if you have some aim. The categorical imperative commands whatever your aims, and Kant says it is the supreme principle of morality.

The universal law formulation tests a maxim, which states an action and its purpose. If the maxim cannot be universalized without contradiction, or you cannot will that everyone act on it, the act is forbidden.

The humanity formulation forbids treating persons merely as means. Persons have dignity as rational agents, and that dignity does not depend on how useful they are. Rachels, chapter 10, calls this respect for persons.

Kantian and utilitarian answers to one case differ in what they ask. Kant asks about the maxim and about respect for persons. The utilitarian asks about consequences, and cannot give a verdict without stated assumptions about them.

vocabulary.definition: A command that applies only if you have a certain aim, such as: if you want a good grade, study.

A failure in which a maxim, universalized, defeats itself, so the act it describes could not exist or achieve its purpose.
A failure in which a universalized maxim is conceivable but a rational agent could not will it, because it would defeat aims the agent must hold.
Act only on a maxim you can will to be a universal law.
Treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means.
The unconditional worth Kant ascribes to persons as rational agents, which has no price and cannot be traded against benefits.

study.overview: Kant holds that morality rests on reason, not on feeling or consequences. Only a good will, which acts from duty, is good without qualification. Kant gives two tests for acts: the universal law formulation asks whether your maxim is coherent, and the humanity formulation asks whether you respect persons. This guide covers both tests and shows how a Kantian answer differs from a utilitarian one on the Latimer case.

points.heading: Duty, imperatives and the good will
points.explanation:
In section I of the Groundwork, Kant says an act has moral worth when it is done from duty, which reason recognizes, and not merely from inclination. Compare two shopkeepers who both give correct change. One does it because honesty is good for business. The other does it from duty. Only the second act has moral worth. Kant does not call feelings bad. He says acting merely from inclination does not give an act moral worth, and feelings may accompany acting from duty.

Kant also separates two kinds of command. A hypothetical imperative applies if you have some aim: if you want a good grade, study. The categorical imperative applies whatever your aims: do not make false promises, whatever you want. Kant calls it the supreme principle of morality.

points.heading: The universal law formulation: testing a maxim
points.explanation:
The formulation says: act only on a maxim you can will to be a universal law. A maxim states an action and its purpose, so the purpose must stay inside the maxim. There are three steps. First, state the maxim as action plus purpose. Second, imagine everyone acting on it. Third, ask whether that is conceivable and whether you could will it.

The test is not utilitarian. It does not ask what would happen if everyone did it. It asks whether the maxim is coherent.

Example of a contradiction in conception: “I will make a promise I do not intend to keep, in order to get a loan.” If everyone did this, the practice of promising would be destroyed, so the purpose of getting a loan fails. The maxim defeats itself. The exam maxim is often said to fail the same way: “I will cheat on an exam when sure not to be caught, in order to get a higher grade.” If everyone cheated whenever they could, a grade would no longer be taken as a sign of what a student knows, so the higher grade would lose the value that was the point of cheating. This verdict is disputed, and the seminar tests it.

Example of a contradiction in will: “I will refuse help to anyone in need, in order to keep all my resources for myself.” A world of universal nonassistance is conceivable. But a rational agent wills the means needed to pursue their ends, and such a world rules out help you may need. So you cannot consistently will it.

By contrast, “I will give money each month to a charity, in order to help people in need” passes. When you work through such cases, a common difficulty is that a maxim can be worded too narrowly or too broadly. Rachels, chapter 9, discusses this and conflicts between rules. Treat these as live objections to the test.

points.heading: The humanity formulation: persons as ends
points.explanation:
The formulation says: treat humanity, in yourself and in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Persons have dignity as rational agents. Dignity has no price and cannot be traded against benefits. It does not depend on how useful a person is.

The key word is “merely”. Kant does not forbid using people. A barista freely agrees to serve a customer, and can share the aim and consent to how she is treated. A lender deceived by a false promise cannot consent to the actual arrangement, because she does not know what it is. So the borrower treats her merely as a means. This is why the false-promise maxim fails the humanity formulation as well as the universal law test. Treating humanity as an end also requires supporting others’ permissible ends where possible and developing our own capacities.

Kant takes the two formulations to give the same verdicts. You may doubt this. A good habit is to note which formulation you find stronger and tie your reason to a passage in the reading.

points.heading: Kant and Mill on the Latimer case
points.explanation:
The two theories ask different questions. Kant asks about the maxim and about respect for persons. For Robert Latimer and his daughter Tracy, a Kantian states the maxim Latimer acted on, tests it under the universal law formulation, and then applies the humanity formulation. Kantians may disagree about how to word the maxim, which shows why wording matters.

The utilitarian asks about consequences, and cannot give a verdict without stated assumptions about them. The answer is therefore a conditional. Before Mill’s principle gives a verdict, you would need to know: Tracy’s future experiences, whether alternatives such as better pain care existed, the effects on the family, and the indirect effects on disabled people and on trust in carers.

A further question of principle is whether grounding dignity in rational agency adequately protects people with profound cognitive disabilities. Possible answers include grounding dignity in capacity, in species membership, or in duties regarding all humans. Treat this as a question of principle, not a judgment of Tracy’s capacities, which the sources do not give. The question to carry forward is what a theory should say when it cannot give a determinate answer.

segments.title: Latimer again: what kind of person?
segments.description:
Return to the Tracy Latimer case and the utilitarian and Kantian answers from the past two weeks.
On the slide, ask: so far we asked whether the act was right. What would we also need to know about Robert Latimer himself, and over what period of time, to judge him?
Take three or four answers aloud, and keep the words students use for his character on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Handle with care; some students may have personal experience of disability. Facts: Latimer, a Saskatchewan farmer, killed his twelve-year-old daughter Tracy in 1993. He was convicted of second-degree murder, and the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the conviction in 2001. Students will offer words like compassionate or desperate. Keep them for later.

segments.title: Character, habit and flourishing
segments.description:
With slides, introduce Aristotle’s account from Nicomachean Ethics, book I, chapter 7: the good for a human being is eudaimonia, activity of the soul in line with virtue. Use this background to explain book II’s account of acquiring virtues of character.
Distinguish intellectual virtue, taught, from moral virtue, or virtue of character, acquired by habituation. Use his analogy: we become builders by building and harpists by playing, so we become just by doing just acts.
Stress his point that doing a just act is not yet being just: the agent must act knowingly, choose the act for its own sake, and act from a firm character. Contrast this with the shopkeeper from last time: Aristotle expects the good person to take pleasure in acting well, where Kant required duty, rather than self-interest or inclination, to be the motivating reason.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: reading habit as mindless routine. Aristotle means practice guided by teachers, later chosen by the agent. Translate eudaimonia as flourishing, not happiness in Mill’s sense. Point to book II, chapters 1 to 4, and Rachels, chapter 12, for the passages; do not quote from memory.

segments.title: The doctrine of the mean
segments.description:
With slides, state the doctrine: a virtue of character is a settled state between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency.

The two student leaders open with the question they prepared: when Aristotle says the mean is what the practically wise person would choose, does the doctrine guide action, or is it circular?

The instructor speaks only to correct a misreading of the text.

segments.title: Your own case: can the virtue ethicist answer it?

Students bring the case they prepared, where asking what a virtuous person would do gives no clear answer or an answer that seems wrong.

Students judge whether the objection is that the theory lacks guidance, or that it gives the wrong verdict.

segments.title: Where do we stand?

The leaders note the answers on the board and ask the group which theory is attracting most students.

keyIdeas: Aristotle changes the question. Utilitarianism and Kant ask which act is right. Aristotle asks what a good person is like, and what it takes to flourish (eudaimonia) as a human being.

Virtues of character are acquired by habituation. We become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, so moral education starts with practice, and the feelings it trains are part of the virtue.

The doctrine of the mean: a virtue of character is a settled state between an excess and a deficiency, such as courage between cowardice and rashness. The mean is relative to the person and the situation, and practical wisdom finds it. Some acts, such as murder, have no mean.

Virtue ethics contrasts with rule-based and consequence-based theories. It does not rest on a single principle, a maxim test or a sum of happiness. It asks what a person of good character, with practical wisdom, would do. Its critics reply that this gives weak guidance for action.
