study.overview: Aristotle changes the question of ethics. Utilitarianism and Kant ask which act is right. Aristotle asks what a good person is like and what it takes to flourish (eudaimonia) as a human being. His answer rests on character: virtues are acquired by habit, and each lies at a mean between two vices. This guide sets out those ideas and shows how they differ from rule-based and consequence-based theories. Read it with Nicomachean Ethics, book II, and Rachels, chapter 12.

points.heading: Virtue is acquired by habit, and the feelings count
points.explanation: Aristotle distinguishes intellectual virtue, which is taught, from moral virtue, or virtue of character, which is acquired by habituation. His analogy: we become builders by building and harpists by playing the harp, so we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts. Habit here is not mindless routine. It is practice guided by teachers, which the agent later chooses for herself. Doing a just act is not yet being just. The agent must act knowingly, choose the act for its own sake, and act from a firm character. The feelings that practice trains are part of the virtue: the good person takes pleasure in acting well. Compare the shopkeeper from last time. Kant required duty, rather than self-interest or inclination, to be the motivating reason. Aristotle expects the good person to enjoy acting well. Example: a child who is made to share, and is helped to see why it matters, gradually comes to share willingly. Eventually she is generous because she cares about others, not because she is told to. Translate eudaimonia as flourishing, not as happiness in Mill’s sense.

points.heading: The doctrine of the mean
points.explanation: A virtue of character is a settled state between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency. Courage lies between cowardice and rashness. Generosity lies between stinginess and prodigality. The same pattern holds for temperance (between self-indulgence and insensibility) and good temper (between irascibility and lack of spirit). The mean is not an arithmetic midpoint and not moderation in everything. It is relative to the person and the situation. Aristotle’s example is the wrestler Milo, whose right amount of food differs from a beginner’s. A soldier’s courage differs from a student’s. The mean for anger differs for a parent and for a referee. Practical wisdom, as the person of good judgment would use it, finds the mean in each situation. Some acts and feelings, such as murder, theft and spite, have no mean, because they are bad in themselves. So there is no right amount of murder. See book II, chapters 6 to 7.

points.heading: Virtue ethics set against rules and consequences
points.explanation: Mill counts consequences. Kant tests maxims. Virtue ethics rests on no single principle and no sum of happiness. It asks what a person of good character, with practical wisdom, would do. Take the murderer at the door: a would-be killer asks where your friend is hiding. Kant held that you still may not lie. A virtue ethicist asks what a person of honesty, loyalty, courage and practical wisdom would do. Three features are distinctive: no single principle, attention to the agent’s whole character, and judgment in the case. Rules guide acts; virtues shape the agent. The same shift appears in the Latimer case. We asked whether his act was right. Virtue ethics also asks what kind of person he was, and over what period of time. Aristotle does not settle the case. He gives a different question, not an algorithm.

points.heading: The main objection: does it guide action?
points.explanation: Critics say the theory gives weak guidance. If the mean is what the practically wise person would choose, the doctrine may be circular. Who counts as wise, and how do we learn to recognize one? Defenders reply that the mean is not an empty phrase. It names the relevant feelings, actions and vices, and the practically wise person weighs competing virtues in context. Rachels, chapter 12, raises the action-guidance objection. Test any objection by asking whether it says the theory lacks guidance or that it gives the wrong verdict. Example: when loyalty to a friend conflicts with honesty, the theory may say only that the wise person would judge well. That is a complaint about guidance. If it told us to do something clearly wrong, that would be a complaint about the verdict. Your paper defending one theory, which counts for 20% of the grade, is due next week. Choose your theory and its strongest objection now.

l_c04d657f883d.summary: Students examine Hobbes's argument that morality is a rational agreement to escape the state of nature.

segments.title: Why follow the rules when no one is watching?
segments.description:
Recall Robert Latimer and his daughter Tracy, and the utilitarian, Kantian and virtue answers given so far.
Ask the room: all three theories say what is right, but why should anyone follow moral rules when no one is watching?
Collect three answers aloud and write them on the board. Return to them at the end of the lecture.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect conscience, fear of punishment, or reciprocity. Do not evaluate yet. Fear and reciprocity are the seeds of Hobbes’s answer, so keep them for the final segment.

segments.title: Hobbes’s state of nature
segments.description:
Present on slides Hobbes’s argument in chapter 13: people are roughly equal in strength and cunning, and they want the same scarce goods.
Set out his three causes of quarrel, competition, diffidence (distrust) and glory, and the war of all against all that follows.
Explain the right of nature: in this condition each person may do whatever preserves their own life.
Students note which parts of the picture are claims about human nature and which follow from having no common power.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: treating the state of nature as a historical period. Hobbes presents it as the condition that would follow if government vanished. Paraphrase his description of life there and point to chapter 13. Do not quote from memory.

segments.title: The laws of nature from self-interest
segments.description:
Present on slides the laws from chapters 14 and 15: seek peace if it can be had; lay down your right to all things if others will too; keep the covenants you make.
Show that each follows from the aim of survival, so that reason, not sympathy, recommends them.
Explain Hobbes’s claim that justice is keeping covenants, so injustice is failing to keep them.
In pairs, students state why the second law is a trade, not a sacrifice.
segments.teacherNotes: Hobbes does not say people are good, or that the laws are commands. They are conclusions of reason about what preserves life. Contrast with Mill and Kant: here morality is justified by self-interest, not by greatest happiness or duty.

segments.title: A worked prisoner’s dilemma, then enforcement
segments.description:
Show on a slide the payoff table for suspects A and B, who agreed to stay silent. In pairs, students find each suspect’s best choice whatever the other does, and compare the result with mutual silence.
Then add a hypothetical enforcement mechanism: suppose any confession is detected with certainty and triggers an additional 6 years of confinement, enforced by a third party. Assume each suspect chooses solely to minimize total years confined. Pairs recompute each suspect’s best choice.
Pairs report whether the penalty changes the choice and why.
segments.teacherNotes:
Years in prison, lower is better.
Both silent: 1 each.
A confesses, B silent: A 0, B 10.
A silent, B confesses: A 10, B 0.
Both confess: 5 each. Confessing wins either way (0<1, 5<10), yet 5 each is worse than 1 each.
With the penalty: A confessing costs 0+6=6 against silent B (silence 1), and 5+6=11 against confessing B (silence 10). Silence wins both ways: 1 each. The penalty must exceed the largest gain, 5.

segments.title: The sovereign, the Fool and an objection
segments.description:
Connect the hypothetical enforcer to Hobbes’s sovereign: a common power that makes breaking covenants cost more than keeping them. Explain that the example models enforcement, not the moral justification of the suspects’ agreement. Present on slides the Fool of chapter 15, who says breaking a covenant is reasonable when you can get away with it, and Hobbes’s reply about reputation.
Present the objection from Rachels, chapter 6: the contract is made by those who can bargain and benefit one another, so those who cannot, such as Tracy Latimer, seem to fall outside morality.
Restate it as premises and a conclusion, then ask whether the best reply answers this objection or a different one.
In pairs, students state one premise in a form its defender would accept, and three pairs say it aloud.
Return to the board answers from the start, sort them into fear, reciprocity and conscience, and say which Hobbes builds on.
Set the seminar task: bring the objection you prepared, its best reply and your verdict. Remind students that the paper defending one theory is due at the end of this week and is scored on the rubric levels A to D.
segments.teacherNotes: Reconstruction: P1 If moral standing rests only on the capacity to participate in mutually beneficial cooperation, beings without that capacity have no moral standing in their own right. P2 Some beings lack that capacity. C Those beings have no moral standing in their own right. Ask whether social contract theory must accept P1. Reply: bargainers may agree to protect beings they care about. Test whether this gives those beings standing in their own right or makes their protection depend on others’ interests. Hobbes’s reply to the Fool: a known covenant-breaker cannot expect others to admit him into any alliance for defense, except by their mistake, so breaking faith is a gamble reason does not recommend. The reply is contested. Treat Tracy as a person, not an illustration. Paper is worth 20%.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: is the state of nature a fact?
segments.description:
Before the seminar, assign the two student leaders this opening question to prepare: does Hobbes’s argument depend on people really being as he describes, or does it work as a thought experiment? The leaders open the discussion with their question.
Students answer one another with evidence from chapter 13 or Rachels, chapter 6.
The instructor intervenes only to ask for the passage.
segments.teacherNotes: Strong answers separate empirical claims (people are roughly equal, distrustful) from the conditional: if there is no common power, then conflict. Seminar participation is worth 10%, so note who cites the text. Instructor exposition under two minutes.

segments.title: The objection you prepared, and the reply
segments.description:
In groups of four, each student presents the objection to social contract theory they prepared from Rachels, chapter 6, or from the lecture.
The group tests whether the best reply answers that objection and decides whether it works.
Each group chooses one objection to put to the room, and a student from that group leads the discussion.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely objections: those excluded from the contract, the Fool, no actual agreement was made, the contract justifies any sovereign. Check that students restate the objection fairly before replying. Prompt weaker groups to name the premise they reject.

segments.title: Latimer again, and where do we stand?
segments.description:
Return to Robert Latimer and his daughter Tracy. Students lead the question: what would a contract theorist say about what Latimer did, and who is protected by the rules?
The leaders keep a board list of what each of the four theories explains and what it leaves out.
Each student then states aloud, in one sentence, whether morality as rational agreement convinces them more than the other theories, and which objection it must still answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Contract theory asks which rules rational agents would accept, not which act has the best result. Rational contractors would plausibly accept protection against killing. Ask both whether Tracy has protection in her own right and whether the agreed rule could permit an exception in her circumstances; neither answer follows simply from her inability to bargain. Keep the objections list for comparing theories on hard cases next time.

keyIdeas: Hobbes (Leviathan, chapter 13) argues that without a common power, people live in a state of nature. Rough equality, competition for scarce goods, mutual distrust and the pursuit of reputation lead to a war of all against all. In that condition there is no industry, no security and no justice.

Hobbes’s laws of nature (chapters 14 and 15) are rules of reason, not commands. Each follows from self-interest in survival: seek peace when you can, give up your right to all things if others do too, and keep your covenants.

The state of nature has the structure of a prisoner’s dilemma. Each person’s best choice alone leaves everyone worse off than cooperation would. Rachels (chapter 6) uses this to show why self-interested people would accept moral rules, and why they need enforcement to make cooperation secure.

Social contract theory treats morality as the rules rational people would agree to for mutual benefit. Its main objection is that it seems to leave out those who cannot bargain or benefit others, such as infants, severely disabled people and animals. Evaluating it means reconstructing the objection and testing the reply, as with the objections to utilitarianism.

vocabulary.definition: Hobbes’s name for the condition of people with no common power over them. Everyone is roughly equal and distrustful, and life is a war of all against all.
In Hobbes, the liberty each person has to use any means to preserve their own life.
In Hobbes, rules found by reason that tell us what preserves life, such as seeking peace and keeping covenants.
An agreement in which one party promises to do something later in return for another’s promise or action.
The common power that Hobbes says is needed to enforce covenants by making breaking them more costly than keeping them.
A situation in which each person’s best choice, whatever the others do, leads to an outcome worse for all than cooperation.
The view that morality is a set of rules that rational people would agree to for their mutual benefit.
Hobbes’s imagined objector in chapter 15, who says it is reasonable to break a covenant when you can profit and escape punishment.

study.overview: Hobbes argues that morality is a rational agreement that lets self-interested people escape a life of constant conflict. Without a common power, people fall into a state of nature. Reason then recommends laws of nature, and a sovereign makes those laws secure. A prisoner’s dilemma shows why enforcement matters. The main objection is that this view seems to leave out beings who cannot bargain, such as Tracy Latimer. Read Leviathan, chapters 13 to 15, and Rachels, chapter 6, alongside this guide.

points.heading: The state of nature is a thought experiment about having no common power
points.explanation: In Leviathan, chapter 13, Hobbes asks what life would be like if government vanished. People are roughly equal in strength and cunning, and they want the same scarce goods. He names three causes of quarrel: competition, diffidence (distrust) and glory (reputation). The result is a war of all against all. Hobbes describes a life with no industry, no security and no justice. In this condition each person has a right of nature to do whatever preserves their own life. Do not read this as a historical period. It is the condition that would follow if there were no common power. Notice which parts are claims about human nature (rough equality, distrust) and which follow from having no common power (constant war). For example, two neighbors who each fear a night raid may each strike first. Neither is wicked. Both are protecting their lives. Paraphrase Hobbes and cite chapter 13; do not quote from memory.

points.heading: The laws of nature are rules of reason that follow from self-interest
points.explanation: In chapters 14 and 15, Hobbes gives laws of nature. They are not commands and they do not assume people are good. They are conclusions of reason about what preserves life. First, seek peace if it can be had. Second, lay down your right to all things if others will too. Third, keep the covenants you make. The second law is a trade, not a sacrifice. You give up the right to attack others, and you get safety from their attacks. Justice, for Hobbes, is keeping covenants. Injustice is failing to keep them. This differs from Mill and Kant. Here morality is justified by self-interest, not by greatest happiness or duty. Example: two farmers agree to stop raiding each other’s barns. Each gives up a right and each gains a safe harvest. In chapter 15, the Fool says breaking a covenant is reasonable when you can get away with it. Hobbes replies that a reputation for breaking covenants costs you future partners. That reply is contested.

points.heading: The prisoner’s dilemma shows why cooperation needs enforcement
points.explanation: Rachels, chapter 6, uses the prisoner’s dilemma to show why self-interested people would accept moral rules. Take suspects A and B, who agreed to stay silent. Years in prison, lower is better. Both silent: 1 each. A confesses, B silent: A 0, B 10. A silent, B confesses: A 10, B 0. Both confess: 5 each. Whatever the other does, confessing is better (0 < 1, and 5 < 10). Yet 5 each is worse than 1 each. Each person’s best choice alone leaves both worse off. Now suppose any confession is detected with certainty and triggers an extra 6 years, enforced by a third party. Confessing against a silent partner costs 0 + 6 = 6, against 1 for silence. Confessing against a confessing partner costs 5 + 6 = 11, against 10 for silence. Silence now wins either way, and both get 1 year. The penalty must exceed the largest gain from confessing, which is 5. This models Hobbes’s sovereign, a common power that makes breaking covenants cost more than keeping them. It models enforcement, not the moral justification of the suspects’ agreement.

points.heading: The main objection: those who cannot bargain seem to fall outside morality
points.explanation: Social contract theory treats morality as the rules rational people would agree to for mutual benefit. Rachels, chapter 6, raises the objection that this seems to leave out those who cannot bargain or benefit others, such as infants, severely disabled people and animals. To assess it, reconstruct it fairly. P1: If moral standing rests only on the capacity to participate in mutually beneficial cooperation, beings without that capacity have no moral standing in their own right. P2: Some beings lack that capacity. C: Those beings have no moral standing in their own right. Consider Tracy Latimer, the daughter of Robert Latimer. Treat her as a person, not an illustration. A possible reply is that bargainers may agree to protect beings they care about. Test this reply. Does it give Tracy standing in her own right, or does her protection depend on other people’s interests? Ask also whether the theory must accept P1. Then check that your reply answers this objection and not a different one.

l_2b4f698572e2.summary: Students run each theory against the trolley cases and see where each gives strained or conflicting verdicts.
suggestedReadings: Philippa Foot, "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect"

segments.title: Switch and footbridge: first verdicts
segments.description:
Show both cases on a slide and ask students to vote by hand before any theory is named.
Switch: a runaway trolley will kill five workers unless you turn it onto a side track, where it will kill one.
Footbridge: a runaway trolley will kill five workers unless you push a heavy stranger off a bridge into its path. His body will stop the trolley, saving the five, but he will die. Assume there is no other way to stop it.
Record the two vote counts on the board and ask two students on opposite sides for one reason each.
segments.teacherNotes: Most students say turn the switch and refuse the push. Keep the counts for the seminar. Do not name any theory yet. Say these cases come from the assigned Thomson paper.

segments.title: Killing and letting die
segments.description:
Define the distinction on a slide and apply it to the switch case.
Turning the switch kills one person. Doing nothing lets five die.
Ask what follows if killing is always worse than letting die, then ask whether that fits our verdict on the bystander.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: saying the bystander who does nothing kills the five. She lets them die. Foot’s idea is that killing one is worse than letting five die; that is why the surgeon may not operate. If that held generally, nobody could turn the switch, so the distinction cannot settle the cases alone. Next time, Singer asks whether letting distant people die is wrong when we could save them.

segments.title: Thomson’s argument: the bystander, the surgeon and the loop
segments.description:
Follow Thomson on slides in order. Section II: the bystander who may turn the trolley, set against a surgeon who may not take one patient’s organs to save five.
Section IV: test the proposal that the difference is using the one as a means, then show the loop variant, which challenges that proposal.
Section V: introduce rights. Sections VI and VII: examine redirecting a threat, with her condition that the means used must not infringe the rights of the one.
End on the point that redirection alone does not separate switch from footbridge.
segments.teacherNotes: Loop case: the side track curves back to the five, and the one person’s body would stop the trolley. Thomson argues that turning remains permissible despite needing the person’s body to stop the trolley. That verdict makes the loop a challenge to the means explanation; ask students whether they accept it. Stress the condition about rights infringed by the means. Explain that Thomson allows that killing the side-track worker infringes his right to life. Turning the switch would do him no wrong if the trolley somehow missed him, whereas pushing the stranger off the bridge itself infringes his rights even if he survives unharmed. Cite sections; do not quote.

segments.title: Run each theory on the two cases
segments.description:
Form four groups, one for each theory studied so far: utilitarian, Kantian, virtue ethics and social contract.
Each group fills in a row of a grid on the board: its theory’s verdict on switch and on footbridge, the reason, and one point where the answer strains.
Groups report in turn and the lecturer marks agreement and conflict between theories on the shared grid.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected answers.
Utilitarian: assuming each person’s survival contributes equally to overall welfare and there are no other differences in consequences, turn and push. State these assumptions to the groups before they deliberate. Strain: distinguishing the cases requires a justified appeal to rules or wider consequences.
Kantian: push uses a person merely as a means; switch contested.
Virtue: consider what compassion, justice, courage and practical wisdom require in each case. Students must defend their verdict rather than assume that recoil settles it; strain: these considerations may not give a clear answer.
Contract: rules each could accept; verdict depends on the rule chosen.

segments.title: Where the theories strain, and how to judge
segments.description:
Take two strained moves from the grid and examine them on slides.
A utilitarian who accepts the push must say our reluctance is a mistake, or appeal to rules and wider consequences.
A Kantian must explain why the switch does not use the one as a means when the push plainly does.
State the test for judging a theory: does it explain why the cases differ? Remind the two student leaders to confirm the opening question they prepared.
segments.teacherNotes: Fair test: a theory’s verdict against intuition is not a refutation; ask what it must say about the intuition. Seminar participation is graded, so every student should arrive with a question or a position on which theory handles the cases best.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: does killing versus letting die matter?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared: the bystander may turn the trolley though she kills one, so does the distinction do any moral work?
The group tests the answer on the surgeon case and on the footbridge push.
The leaders keep the discussion moving, and the instructor intervenes only to correct misreadings of Thomson.
segments.teacherNotes: No slides in the seminar. If discussion stalls, ask whether the surgeon case differs because he kills or because of the means he uses. If someone calls the distinction meaningless, ask what the surgeon would say.

segments.title: Loop, means and rights
segments.description:
Students argue whether using someone as a means explains why the footbridge push is wrong, and what the loop case does to that explanation.
They then ask whether Thomson’s condition about rights infringed by the means does better.
Students connect the humanity formulation from the Kant discussion to the footbridge case.
segments.teacherNotes: Strong answer: the loop shows that using someone as a means cannot be the whole explanation, so Thomson turns to rights. Weak answer: saying redirection alone settles it. Ask students to restate the condition in their own words and cite sections.

segments.title: Which theory handles the cases best?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, which theory best handles the switch and footbridge cases and the strongest objection it must still answer.
The group notes where positions cluster and challenges the best-supported view.
Anyone may change position and say why. The instructor ends with a minute on where the group stands.
segments.teacherNotes: Test against the three criteria: firm verdicts, explaining the difference, no strained moves. Do not push toward one answer. A good reply admits the cost of its theory. Next time, Singer asks whether letting distant people die is wrong when we could save them at small cost.

keyIdeas: Thomson, “The Trolley Problem”, asks why a bystander may turn a trolley from five people onto one, while a surgeon may not cut up one healthy patient to save five. The bystander challenge begins in section II. Section IV tests the proposal that the difference lies in using someone as a means, and her loop variant puts that proposal under pressure. Section V introduces rights. Sections VI and VII take up the redirection of a threat, with the condition that the means used must not infringe the rights of the person it falls on.

Redirection alone does not separate the switch case from the footbridge case. In both, a threat to five is moved to one. What differs is how the one is affected: in the switch case he is on the side track, while in the footbridge case a stranger is pushed and his body is the means of stopping the trolley.

Turning the switch kills one person. Not turning it lets five die. If killing one were always worse than letting five die, the bystander could not turn the switch, so the distinction cannot by itself explain our verdicts on the cases.

Each theory studied so far strains on the cases. Utilitarianism gives the same count of lives for switch and footbridge. Kant’s humanity formulation condemns the footbridge push more clearly than the switch. Virtue ethics and social contract theory give verdicts that depend on how their central questions are answered.

To judge which theory handles the cases best, ask three things. Does it deliver the verdicts we hold most firmly? Does it explain why the cases differ? Does it do so without strained moves, or does it tell us to give up the judgment instead?

study.overview: This lesson ran the two trolley cases against each theory studied so far. In the switch case you turn a runaway trolley onto a side track, where it kills one worker instead of five. In the footbridge case you push a heavy stranger off a bridge so that his body stops the trolley. Most people turn the switch and refuse the push, and Thomson, “The Trolley Problem”, asks why. No theory explained the difference cleanly, so the useful skill is judging how well each one copes. Use the points below to review the distinction between killing and letting die, Thomson’s argument, and the test for comparing theories.

points.heading: Killing and letting die cannot settle the cases alone
points.explanation: Killing is causing someone’s death. Letting die is failing to prevent a death you could have prevented. Turning the switch kills one worker. Doing nothing lets five die. If killing one were always worse than letting five die, the bystander could never turn the switch, yet most of us think she may. So the distinction cannot by itself explain our verdicts. A common mistake is to say the bystander who does nothing kills the five. She lets them die. Keep the two terms apart. Next time, Singer asks whether letting distant people die can be as wrong as failing to save a child in front of you.

points.heading: Thomson: redirection, means and rights
points.explanation: Thomson asks why a bystander may turn the trolley from five onto one, while a surgeon may not cut up one healthy patient to save five (the bystander challenge begins in section II). In section IV she tests the proposal that the difference lies in using someone as a means. Her loop variant puts that proposal under pressure. In the loop case the side track curves back to the five, and the one person’s body would stop the trolley. Thomson argues that turning is still permissible, so using a person as a means cannot be the whole explanation. Section V introduces rights. Sections VI and VII examine redirecting a threat, with the condition that the means used must not infringe the rights of the person it falls on. Redirection alone does not separate the cases, since in both a threat to five is moved to one. What differs is how the one is affected. The side-track worker is simply in the trolley’s path. The pushed stranger’s own body is the means, and pushing him infringes his rights even if he survives unharmed.

points.heading: How each theory strains on the cases
points.explanation: Each theory studied so far strains somewhere. Utilitarianism, assuming each life contributes equally to welfare and the consequences are otherwise the same, counts five lives against one in both cases and says turn and push. To resist the push it must appeal to rules or wider consequences, or say our reluctance is a mistake. Kant’s humanity formulation condemns the push more clearly, since the stranger is used merely as a means. But the Kantian must still explain why the switch does not use the one as a means when the push plainly does. Virtue ethics asks what compassion, justice, courage and practical wisdom require, and you must defend a verdict rather than assume that recoil settles it. Those considerations may not give a clear answer. Social contract theory asks which rules each person could accept, so its verdict depends on the rule chosen.

points.heading: Judging which theory handles the cases best
points.explanation: A theory’s verdict against intuition is not by itself a refutation. Ask what the theory must say about that intuition. Then apply three questions. Does it deliver the verdicts we hold most firmly? Does it explain why the cases differ? Does it do so without strained moves, or does it tell us to give up the judgment instead? For example, a utilitarian who accepts the push must call our reluctance a mistake or appeal to rules and wider consequences. That is a cost, and a good answer admits it. When you state a position, name the theory, say why it handles the two cases best, and give the strongest objection it must still answer.

l_022cc6a710bd.title: What we owe distant strangers: Singer
l_022cc6a710bd.summary: Students assess Singer's argument that affluent people must give until further giving would cost something of comparable moral importance.
suggestedReadings: Peter Singer, The Life You Can Save
Garrett Hardin, "Lifeboat Ethics: The Case Against Helping the Poor"

segments.title: The pond and the distant child: first verdicts
segments.description:
Show two cases on a slide and ask for a vote by hand before Singer is named.
Case one: you pass a shallow pond where a small child is drowning, and wading in will ruin your shoes and trousers. Case two: suppose giving the same amount to an aid agency would save a child you will never meet.
Recall the earlier social contract discussion: the contract theorist struggled to say who is owed anything when the other party cannot bargain. Ask what, if anything, differs between the cases.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect near-unanimous yes to case one and a split on case two. List the differences students give (distance, certainty, other helpers) on the board. Return to this list when Singer’s second claim is introduced. Do not name the principle yet.

segments.title: Singer’s argument and the two principles
segments.description:
Place the paper in its context: Singer wrote it in response to the 1971 famine and refugee crisis in East Bengal.
Present on slides the three-step argument: want causes suffering and death, which are bad; the principle of preventing bad things when nothing of comparable moral importance is lost; the application to giving.
State the strong and moderate principles side by side. Explain that the strong principle applies to each further donation: we must keep giving while further giving prevents harm without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance. Ask students to identify what would justify stopping. Then present Singer’s claims that distance and the number of other possible helpers do not change what we ought to do.
segments.teacherNotes: Paraphrase Singer; quote only from the text students hold. Common mistake: calling the paper simply utilitarian. Singer says most people already accept the principle, whatever their theory. The pond case is evidence for the principle, not a separate premise.

segments.title: Rebuild the drowning child argument
segments.description:
In pairs, students receive six cards and label each as a premise, an illustration or a conclusion.
They draw arrows showing which cards support which, and say which cards the conclusion actually depends on.
Each pair compares its diagram with a neighboring pair. The instructor then shows on a slide that several orders display the same valid reasoning, and asks what stays fixed in all of them.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards and roles:
A. Suffering and death from lack of food, shelter and medical care are bad. Premise.
B. If we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Premise.
C. If I can save a drowning child at the cost of muddy clothes, I ought to wade in. Illustration of B, not an independent premise.
D. Distance, and other possible helpers, do not change what I ought to do. Supporting claim: it blocks the reply that B does not reach distant people or cases where others could help. It defends applying B to the famine, not E’s factual claim that giving works.
E. By giving to famine relief I can prevent such suffering without sacrificing anything of comparable importance. Premise.
F. Therefore I ought to give. Conclusion.
Mark dependencies, not order: F needs A, B and E; D defends applying B to the famine case; C supports B.

segments.title: The charity objection and a worked case
segments.description:
Work one hypothetical case on a slide. A family pays $20,000 a year for private school; moving the child to a good public school means losing the private school’s smaller classes and music program, but the child is still educated. Suppose the same $20,000 would pay for treatment that prevents several children’s deaths from a curable illness.
Students compare the two quantities under the strong principle: is a reduced schooling advantage comparable to the death of a child? Then ask whether the moderate principle gives the same verdict.
Present the objection that giving is charity and so optional, Singer’s reply that it is a duty, and the terms supererogatory act and demandingness objection.
segments.teacherNotes: Figures are hypothetical, not real data. Expected: schooling is important, but the comparison is between this specific loss and a child’s death, which ends all future goods; so the loss is not comparable and the strong principle says give. The moderate principle may excuse the family if the loss counts as morally significant. Contested.

segments.title: Which premise would you resist?
segments.description:
In groups of three, students pick the premise of Singer’s argument most open to challenge.
Each group writes the objection and the best reply Singer could give on a shared sheet.
Three groups report, and the class votes by hand on which premise was chosen most and which reply was strongest.
Name the two student leaders and confirm their prepared seminar question: if giving is a duty, why do we praise donors as generous?
segments.teacherNotes: Likely choices: the comparability threshold, the irrelevance of distance, whether donations really work. Common mistake: attacking the conclusion because it is demanding without naming a premise. Ask which premise carries the demand. Groups keep sheets for the seminar. Preparation counts toward seminar participation (10%).

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: duty or charity?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with their prepared question: if Singer is right, why do we praise donors as generous rather than blame those who give nothing?
The instructor adds a brief framing of supererogation and then steps back.
Students respond to each other, citing the text of the paper and the pond case.
segments.teacherNotes: Instructor exposition under two minutes. Listen for confusion between what is praiseworthy and what is required. Singer holds that calling giving charity hides that it is a duty. If discussion stalls, send leaders back to the pond case. Let a contract-theory voice appear if students raise it.

segments.title: The premise you prepared, and the reply
segments.description:
In groups of four, each student presents the premise they would resist and the best reply Singer could give.
The group chooses the strongest objection and states what it would take to answer it.
Each group reports to the room, and students question each other.
Students then say which earlier theory, utilitarian, Kantian, virtue or contract, gives the firmest ground for a duty to give.
segments.teacherNotes: Move among groups without leading. Strong objections: a friend’s child differs from a stranger, uncertainty that aid works, the threshold being too demanding. Push each speaker to separate the premise attacked from the conclusion disliked. Do not reteach the theories. Hold justice and institutions for next time.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, the premise they would resist.
They add the strongest reply Singer could give.
The instructor tallies the premises on the board and notes that next time the question moves from what individuals owe to what justice requires of states and institutions.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept any premise if it is named and the reply is relevant. Ask anyone who says only ‘too demanding’ which premise carries the demand. The tally shows which premise is most contested. Students may build the weekly reading response (20%) on one premise and one reply.

keyIdeas: Singer’s drowning child argument has three parts. Suffering and death from lack of food, shelter and medical care are bad. If we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Giving to famine relief is such a case, so we ought to give.
The pond case supports the principle by appeal to a verdict almost everyone holds. Singer then argues that distance, and the number of other people who could help, do not change what we ought to do.

Singer’s strong principle sets the threshold at sacrificing something of comparable moral importance. His moderate principle sets it at sacrificing something morally significant. The strong version is far more demanding, so the choice of version matters for every later objection.

The objection that charity is optional says giving is generous but not required. Singer replies that giving is a duty. Evaluating the objection means asking whether some gifts are supererogatory and whether the argument asks too much.

Evaluating an argument means finding the premise that carries the most weight and is easiest to challenge, then testing the best reply. Candidates are the comparability threshold, the claim that distance is irrelevant, and the claim that our gifts really prevent the harm.

What would justify stopping?
slides.notes: State the two principles side by side. The strong version is far more demanding, so the choice of version matters for every later objection. Under the strong principle we must keep giving while each further donation prevents harm without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance. Ask students what would justify stopping. Then present Singer’s two further claims: distance does not change what we ought to do, and neither does the number of other people who could help. Return to the board list from the opening vote.

slides.title: Rebuilding the argument: what stays fixed
bullets: Premise: want and death are bad
Premise: the prevention principle
Illustration: the pond supports the principle
Supporting claim: distance and other helpers are irrelevant
Conclusion: therefore I ought to give
slides.notes: Pairs sort six cards into premise, illustration or conclusion, draw arrows, and say what the conclusion depends on. Then show on a slide that several orders display the same valid reasoning. Mark dependencies, not order. The conclusion needs the badness premise, the principle, and the premise that giving prevents such suffering at no comparable cost. The claim about distance and other helpers defends applying the principle to distant famine victims; it does not show that giving works. The pond case supports the principle and is not an independent premise.

slides.title: Worked case: school fees or lives?
bullets: A family pays $20,000 a year for private school.
A good public school means losing smaller classes and a music program.
The same $20,000 would pay for treatment preventing several children’s deaths.
Strong principle: is the loss comparable? Moderate principle?
slides.notes: The figures are hypothetical, not real data. Under the strong principle, schooling matters, but the child remains educated, while a death ends all future goods. So the loss is not comparable and the strong principle says give. The moderate principle may excuse the family if the loss counts as morally significant. This is contested. Then present the objection that giving is charity and so optional, and Singer’s reply that it is a duty. Introduce the terms supererogatory act and demandingness objection.

slides.title: Which premise would you resist?
bullets: The comparability threshold
The claim that distance is irrelevant
The claim that our gifts really prevent the harm
Name the premise, state the objection, give Singer’s best reply
slides.notes: In groups of three, students pick the premise most open to challenge and write the objection and the best reply Singer could give on a shared sheet. Three groups report; the class votes by hand on which premise was chosen most and which reply was strongest. Common mistake: attacking the conclusion because it is demanding without naming a premise. Ask which premise carries the demand. Groups keep their sheets for the seminar. Name the two student leaders and confirm their prepared question: if giving is a duty, why do we praise donors as generous? Preparation counts toward seminar participation (10%). Next time the question moves from what individuals owe to what justice requires of states and institutions.

study.overview: This session tested Singer’s argument that affluent people must give until further giving would cost something of comparable moral importance. You began with a pond case and a distant-child case, rebuilt the argument from its parts, applied it to a worked case about private school fees, and chose the premise you would resist. Use this guide to check that you can state the argument, separate the two principles, judge the charity objection, and defend a choice of weakest premise.

points.heading: The structure of the drowning child argument
points.explanation: Singer’s argument has three parts. Premise one: suffering and death from lack of food, shelter and medical care are bad. Premise two: if we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Premise three: giving to famine relief is such a case. The conclusion is that we ought to give. The pond case is not a separate premise. It is evidence for the second premise, because almost everyone agrees you must wade in to save a drowning child even if it ruins your shoes and trousers. Singer then adds a supporting claim: distance, and the number of other people who could help, do not change what we ought to do. This defends applying the principle to distant famine victims. In your card exercise, the conclusion depended on the first, second and third premises, the distance claim defended applying the principle to the famine case, and the pond case supported the second. Order on the page can change. The dependencies stay fixed. A common mistake is to call the paper simply utilitarian. Singer says most people already accept his principle, whatever their ethical theory.

points.heading: The strong and moderate principles
points.explanation: Singer states two versions of his principle. The strong version sets the threshold at sacrificing something of comparable moral importance. The moderate version sets it at sacrificing something morally significant. The strong version is far more demanding. It applies to each further donation, so we must keep giving while more giving prevents harm without costing us anything of comparable moral importance. Consider the hypothetical family that pays $20,000 a year for private school. Moving the child to a good public school costs the smaller classes and the music program, but the child is still educated. Suppose the same $20,000 would pay for treatment that prevents several children’s deaths from a curable illness. Under the strong principle, a reduced schooling advantage is not comparable to a child’s death, which ends all future goods. So the family ought to give. The moderate principle may excuse the family if the schooling loss counts as morally significant. Which verdict is right is contested. The point is that your choice of version shapes every later objection.

points.heading: The objection that charity is optional
points.explanation: The objection says giving is generous but not required. We praise donors, but we do not blame those who give nothing. Singer replies that giving is a duty, and that calling it charity hides this fact. To evaluate the objection, use two ideas from class. A supererogatory act is one that is good but beyond duty. The demandingness objection says a moral principle asks too much of ordinary people. Ask whether some gifts really are supererogatory, for example a gift far beyond the point where giving costs something comparable. Ask too whether praise and duty can go together. Praising a rescuer at the pond does not show that rescuing was optional. Be careful not to confuse what is praiseworthy with what is required. If you answer only that the conclusion is too demanding, you have not yet identified a premise. Ask which premise carries the demand.

points.heading: Choosing the premise to resist
points.explanation: To evaluate an argument, find the premise that carries the most weight and is easiest to challenge, then test the best reply. Three candidates came up. The first is the comparability threshold: is the loss really not comparable? The second is the claim that distance is irrelevant: perhaps a friend’s child differs morally from a stranger. The third is the claim that our gifts really prevent the harm: perhaps aid does not work as hoped, given uncertainty. For each, state the objection and then the best reply Singer could give. For example, against distance, Singer can point back to the pond case and ask what morally relevant difference distance makes if the child is equally in need. Keep the premise you attack separate from the conclusion you dislike. A strong answer names the premise, gives the objection, states the reply, and says what it would take to answer the objection. You can build your weekly reading response on one premise and one reply.

l_406bbfd465f1.title: Global justice: Nagel
l_406bbfd465f1.summary: Students ask whether duties of justice reach beyond the state, and compare Nagel's view with Singer's duty of beneficence.
readings: Thomas Nagel, "The Problem of Global Justice"
suggestedReadings: John Rawls, The Law of Peoples
Thomas Pogge, World Poverty and Human Rights
Charles Beitz, Political Theory and International Relations

segments.title: Fellow citizen or distant stranger: first verdicts
segments.description:
Show two cases on a slide. In the first, a fellow citizen in your own town cannot afford insulin. In the second, a stranger abroad has the same need and the same cost would meet it.
Ask for a vote by hand, before Nagel is named: do we owe the fellow citizen justice? Do we owe the stranger justice, or only humanity?
Recall Singer’s pond from last time and ask whether his argument treats the two cases alike.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect a split. Many students will say the cases differ but cannot say why. Record the vote on the board and return to it in the final segment of the lecture. Do not name Nagel’s answer yet.

segments.title: Nagel’s argument: justice depends on shared institutions
segments.description:
Set out the problem Nagel starts from: the Hobbesian point that without a sovereign to enforce rules there is no justice, only a state of nature.
Explain his political conception. A state makes laws in citizens’ name and enforces them on citizens by coercion. Citizens are therefore joint authors and subjects of those laws, and that relation grounds the demand that the law treat each citizen’s claims fairly.
Explain why Nagel says no such relation holds across borders. There is no global sovereign. The United Nations has some binding powers, but it does not govern the world’s population as a sovereign state governs its citizens.
Close by stating the claim as a short argument on the slide and marking which premise carries the weight.
segments.teacherNotes: Paraphrase Nagel and send students to the opening discussion of Hobbes and Rawls in the reading. Common mistake: hearing Nagel as saying foreigners do not matter. He says they matter, but under a different kind of duty. Say so early.

segments.title: Justice, humanity and the cosmopolitan reply
segments.description:
Contrast duties of justice with duties of humanity. Justice asks for fair and equal terms among people bound by shared institutions. Humanity asks everyone to avoid cruelty and to relieve desperate need.
Place Singer beside Nagel. Singer’s strong and moderate principles make distance irrelevant, while Nagel makes the strength of our duties depend on our relation to the person.
Present the cosmopolitan critics’ two main replies: birth is morally arbitrary, and global trade and finance rules already bind and shape lives.
State Nagel’s response to each, without judging it yet.
segments.teacherNotes: Nagel’s reply: arbitrariness of birth explains why inequality troubles us, but not that it is an injustice without shared institutions. Treaties between states are agreements among sovereigns, not laws we author. He adds that justice beyond the state would need new global institutions, which he expects to begin as unjust structures of power and only later face demands for legitimacy. Students decide whether this suffices.

segments.title: Justice or humanity? Sorting cases as Nagel would
segments.description:
In pairs, students receive five short claims on a slide. For each they decide whether Nagel would call the duty one of justice or one of humanity, and give a one-line reason.
Pairs then compare answers with a neighboring pair and note any disagreement.
Take two disputed items in the whole group and ask how Singer would answer the same item.
Return to the opening vote and ask who would now change their hand.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers:
1. A state denies one group of its own citizens equal legal protection. Justice, owed among fellow citizens.
2. A stranger abroad is starving after a flood and we can send aid. Humanity.
3. Citizens pay taxes so every citizen’s child gets a school place. Justice, within the state.
4. People in a poor country claim a fair share of the world’s wealth as a matter of justice, not charity. Cosmopolitans agree. Nagel says it is not justice, since no shared sovereign makes both peoples joint authors of common laws; humanity still requires relieving desperate need.
5. A foreign government tortures its own people. A violation of the humanity minimum.

segments.title: Leaders’ questions: can we wrong a stranger or only fail to help?
segments.description:
The two student leaders open with the question they prepared in advance. If distant strangers are owed only humanity, can we ever wrong them, or can we only fail to help them?
Leaders call on classmates, ask for textual support from Nagel, and press for a reply.
The instructor intervenes only to ask for the passage a claim rests on.
segments.teacherNotes: Leaders prepare and circulate the question beforehand, as for the earlier seminars. Seminar participation is graded, so leaders should invite quieter students. A strong answer separates wronging someone from treating them unjustly: failing in humanity can still be a serious wrong.

segments.title: Do global institutions weaken Nagel’s claim?
segments.description:
In groups of four, students take the cosmopolitan objection that trade rules and global financial institutions already coerce people across borders.
Each group decides whether these institutions place people across borders in the dual role of subjects and joint authors, or whether coercion alone should ground duties of justice.
Groups write nothing for collection. Each prepares to state its verdict and the strongest reply to it.
segments.teacherNotes: Possible lines: these bodies bind states by agreement, not citizens as joint authors; or coercion without authorship still raises claims of justice, as critics argue. Push each group to name which premise its reply attacks. Allow disagreement to stand.

segments.title: Nagel against Singer: where do we stand?
segments.description:
Bring the groups together. Each reports its verdict and the strongest reply to it.
Ask the class which view better explains the opening cases: the insulin cases at home and abroad.
Then ask whether Nagel’s humanity minimum could still require as much giving as Singer’s moderate principle.
segments.teacherNotes: Aim for a clear disagreement, not consensus. A good answer to the last question notes that Nagel leaves its details open but limits required aid to helping without serious sacrifice of our own ends, so the two views may differ less in practice than in what they call the failure. Keep the instructor to two or three short interventions.

segments.title: One sentence, and the paper
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, whether Nagel’s reply to the cosmopolitan critics succeeds and the objection he must still answer.
The instructor notes that the Nagel and Singer question can be a topic for the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%), and reminds students to bring the same disciplined premise-and-reply structure to it.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep sentences oral, as last time, and collect nothing. Students may use this week’s reading response (20% of the grade, all responses together) to develop their sentence further.

keyIdeas: Nagel argues that duties of justice depend on shared institutions. A sovereign state acts in its citizens’ name and enforces its rules on them by coercion, and citizens are both its joint authors and its subjects. That relation, he claims, is what makes them owe one another fair treatment.

Nagel separates duties of justice from duties of humanity. Humanity covers a minimal morality owed to every person: do not treat people cruelly, and help those in desperate need. It does not demand that people everywhere be made equal.

Singer’s duty of beneficence and Nagel’s view can agree that we must help distant people in extreme need. They differ over what failing to help is. For Singer, distance is irrelevant and the duty is strong. For Nagel, it is a failure of humanity, not an injustice, and its weight is limited.

Cosmopolitan critics reply that birth in a poor country is morally arbitrary. They add that global trade rules and institutions already shape lives, so justice cannot stop at the border. Assessing Nagel means asking whether his reply meets these points: that justice needs a sovereign, that no global sovereign exists, and that justice beyond the state must wait for new global institutions.

vocabulary.definition: Obligations of fair and equal treatment that, on Nagel’s view, hold among people bound together by shared coercive institutions.
A minimal morality owed to every person: avoid cruelty and relieve desperate need. These duties do not depend on shared institutions; they can still be stringent.

Nagel’s view that the strong duties of justice, such as fair distribution of resources, arise only between people joined by a sovereign state’s institutions. It still allows duties of humanity to all and some standards of fair dealing among states.
The view that duties of justice hold among all persons, whatever their state or citizenship, so that borders do not limit them.
The relation of citizens to a state’s laws: the laws are made in their name and enforced on them. Nagel treats this as the basis of special duties of justice.
A single world authority able to make and enforce law over all states. Nagel notes that none exists.

Does the absence of a global sovereign settle it?

Then return to the opening vote and ask who would now change their hand. Next, the pairs activity: five short claims, sorted as Nagel would, justice or humanity. Today’s seminar then takes up whether we can wrong a stranger or only fail to help.

study.overview: This lesson asked whether duties of justice reach beyond the state. Nagel says they do not, because justice depends on shared institutions. He still holds that we owe every person a minimal morality, which he calls humanity. You compared his view with Singer’s duty of beneficence and weighed Nagel’s reply to the cosmopolitan critics. The opening cases are a useful test throughout: a fellow citizen in your own town who cannot afford insulin, and a stranger abroad with the same need, where the same cost would meet it.

points.heading: Justice depends on shared institutions
points.explanation: Nagel starts from the Hobbesian point that without a sovereign to enforce rules there is no justice, only a state of nature. His political conception applies this to the state. A state makes laws in its citizens’ name and enforces them on citizens by coercion. Citizens are therefore both joint authors and subjects of those laws. That relation, he claims, is what grounds the demand that the law treat each citizen’s claims fairly. Across borders there is no such relation. There is no global sovereign, and the United Nations has some binding powers but does not govern the world’s population as a state governs its citizens. The argument runs: (1) duties of justice require a shared sovereign institution; (2) no global sovereign exists; (3) so there are no global duties of justice. Premise 1 carries the weight, so any serious objection has to attack it. Example: the neighbor who cannot afford insulin lives under laws made in her name and enforced on her. Fairness among citizens is therefore at stake. The stranger abroad does not live under our state’s laws. Be careful not to read Nagel as saying foreigners do not matter. He says they matter, but under a different kind of duty.

points.heading: Duties of justice and duties of humanity
points.explanation: Justice asks for fair and equal terms among people who are bound together by shared institutions. Humanity is a minimal morality owed to every person: do not treat people cruelly, and help those in desperate need. It does not demand that people everywhere be made equal. You sorted cases as Nagel would. A state that denies one group of its own citizens equal legal protection commits an injustice, owed among fellow citizens. Taxes that give every citizen’s child a school place are also a matter of justice within the state. A stranger abroad starving after a flood is a matter of humanity, and so is a foreign government torturing its own people, since that violates the humanity minimum. The disputed case is a claim that people in poor countries are owed a fair share of the world’s wealth as a matter of justice. Cosmopolitans say yes. Nagel says no, because no shared sovereign makes people in both countries joint authors of common laws. Humanity still requires relieving desperate need. A further question from the leaders’ discussion: if strangers are owed only humanity, can we wrong them or only fail to help them? A strong answer separates wronging someone from treating them unjustly. Failing in humanity can still be a serious wrong, even if it is not an injustice.

points.heading: Nagel and Singer compared
points.explanation: The two views can agree that we must help distant people in extreme need. They differ over what failing to help is. For Singer, distance is irrelevant, and the duty is strong. His strong and moderate principles apply the same way to a child in a pond nearby and a child far away. For Nagel, the strength of our duties depends on our relation to the person. Failing to help a distant stranger is a failure of humanity, not an injustice, and its weight is limited. Apply this to the insulin cases. Singer treats the neighbor and the stranger alike, since the same cost would meet the same need. Nagel treats the neighbor as owed justice and the stranger as owed humanity. The two may differ less in practice than in what they call the failure. Nagel leaves the details open, but he limits required aid to helping without serious sacrifice of our own ends. That may be close to what Singer’s moderate principle asks. When you write about this contrast, state clearly which duty each philosopher claims and why.

points.heading: Assessing Nagel’s reply to the cosmopolitans
points.explanation: Cosmopolitan critics make two main replies. First, birth in a poor country is morally arbitrary, so inequality between countries cannot simply be accepted. Second, global trade and finance rules already bind and shape lives, so justice cannot stop at the border. Nagel’s responses are these. The arbitrariness of birth explains why inequality troubles us. It does not show that the inequality is an injustice when there are no shared institutions. Treaties between states are agreements among sovereigns, not laws that individuals author. He adds that justice beyond the state would need new global institutions. He expects these to begin as unjust structures of power and only later face demands for legitimacy. To assess him, ask whether this meets the objections. A critic can accept that these bodies bind states by agreement rather than citizens as joint authors, yet argue that coercion without authorship still raises claims of justice. That reply attacks premise 1, the claim that justice needs a sovereign. Others may find Nagel’s position stable, because the global institutions do not make people joint authors. Disagreement is reasonable here. A good evaluation names which premise it attacks and states the strongest reply to its own verdict. You can bring this structure to the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%). The Nagel and Singer question is one possible topic. This week’s reading response is a place to develop your one-sentence verdict further.

l_510283796d81.title: The moral status of animals
l_510283796d81.summary: Students weigh Singer's equal consideration of interests against Cohen's argument that animals lack rights.
readings: Carl Cohen, "The Case for the Use of Animals in Biomedical Research"
suggestedReadings: Tom Regan, The Case for Animal Rights
Peter Singer, Animal Liberation
Mary Midgley, Animals and Why They Matter

homework.toward: Argumentative paper on an applied question

segments.title: Pain is pain, or is it?
segments.description:
Two claims go on the slide. (A) The same pain matters more when a human feels it than when a pig does. (B) A pain matters the same whoever feels it.
Students vote by show of hands, then two students defend a side in a sentence each.
The lecturer links the split to last time, when Nagel distinguished duties of humanity from duties of justice: suffering matters even without membership in a shared state. The question today is whether species is relevant.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect most to accept A and also say animal cruelty is wrong. Do not resolve it. Name the tension and carry it into Singer’s argument.

segments.title: Singer and Cohen: two answers on moral standing
segments.description:
Set out Singer’s argument from “All Animals Are Equal” as numbered steps on slides. Equal consideration of interests is the basic principle of equality, and sentience is the only defensible boundary for having interests. Preferring one’s own species without a relevant difference is speciesism, parallel to racism and sexism. Equal consideration does not mean equal treatment: a dog has no interest in voting.
Then present Cohen’s argument from “The Case for the Use of Animals in Biomedical Research”. Rights are claims pressed within a moral community of beings who exercise free moral judgment and accept duties. Animals cannot, so they hold no rights, and Cohen denies that favoring humans is a prejudice.
Put one case on the slide: a drug trial could save many human lives but causes severe pain to twenty primates. The lecturer shows where the two authors part: the basis of moral standing, or what that standing implies.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistakes: Singer wants identical treatment; Cohen thinks animal pain does not matter. Cohen rejects rights, not all duties. Trial case: Singer counts the primates’ suffering equally; Cohen finds no right violated if needless suffering is avoided. Paraphrase; send students to the text.

segments.title: Rebuild Cohen’s argument
segments.description:
In groups of three, students receive six statements from Cohen’s argument, shuffled, on a slide or handout.
They arrange the core argument, mark the conclusion, identify the reply to an objection, and identify the separate claim about duties concerning suffering.
Groups compare orders with a neighboring group, then the lecturer shows one order.
segments.teacherNotes:
Statements, in expected order:
1. Rights are claims that only members of a moral community can hold and press.
2. Members of that community can make free moral judgments and accept duties.
3. Animals cannot do this, so they are not members.
4. Infants and severely impaired humans belong, since they are of a kind whose normal members can.
5. So animals have no rights, and research on them violates none.
6. Cohen still grants that needless suffering is wrong.
Statement 5 is the conclusion. Statement 4 answers the marginal cases objection. Statement 6 states a separate duty concerning suffering; it is not a premise supporting statement 5.

segments.title: Replies to Cohen, and choosing one for the seminar
segments.description:
Introduce the argument from marginal cases. If moral judgment is the test, some humans fail it, so either they lose rights or the test is wrong. Cohen replies that standing goes with the kind of being, not the individual.
Set out two ways to press the reply. First, why is the human kind the relevant kind and not the kind of creature that can suffer? Second, Regan’s view that rights belong to every subject of a life, so rights need no moral agency. For each, show what it targets in Cohen’s argument and what Cohen could say back.
Students then choose by show of hands the reply they will test in the seminar. Remind them to bring their prepared discussion questions, since the leaders’ questions count toward seminar participation (10%). Animals is also one of the applied questions open for the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%).
segments.teacherNotes: Cohen’s likely rejoinder to the first: kind membership is not arbitrary because the kind has the capacity at the core of rights. A strong evaluation asks whether that explains why an individual lacking the capacity has rights. If everyone picks the marginal cases reply, assign some to defend Regan so the seminar has two sides.

segments.title: Leaders open: the two arguments restated
segments.description:
The instructor names the two student leaders, who recall the questions they prepared. One asks whether speciesism is a prejudice like racism. The other asks whether Cohen’s moral community argument can include infants.
The leaders restate Singer’s charge of speciesism and Cohen’s argument from moral community, briefly and without notes.
Others correct or add. The instructor asks only where in the text a step is made.
segments.teacherNotes: Check beforehand that the two questions differ so there are two threads. Listen for the usual errors: Singer wants identical treatment, Cohen thinks animal pain does not matter. Let students correct each other first.

segments.title: Leaders’ question: is speciesism a prejudice?
segments.description:
The first leader asks whether favoring humans over animals is a prejudice like racism, or a response to a morally relevant difference.
Students answer each other and cite Singer’s comparison and Cohen’s claim about kinds. The leader keeps the group on what a relevant difference would have to be.
segments.teacherNotes: Push for a test: what would make a difference relevant? Capacity to suffer, moral agency and kind are the candidates. Watch for slides from does it matter to does it deserve equal treatment. A student’s own case, such as farming or an insect of uncertain sentience, can test Singer’s boundary.

segments.title: Leaders’ question: does any reply to Cohen succeed?
segments.description:
The second leader asks whether the argument from marginal cases, or Regan’s subject-of-a-life view, defeats Cohen’s argument.
Students defend and test one reply each, and say what Cohen could answer.
The group decides whether Cohen’s appeal to kind is principled or ad hoc.
segments.teacherNotes: Test each reply by naming the premise it breaks. Press on costs: if the reply works, which humans or animals gain or lose standing? Cohen’s reading of kind may hold or fail depending on whether the group accepts that capacities belong to kinds.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, whether Cohen’s argument succeeds and which reply to it they find strongest.
The instructor notes the split on the board and does not comment. Next time moves to a new applied question.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep each statement to a sentence. A good answer names a premise and a reason. If it names neither, ask which premise the student means.

keyIdeas: Singer’s charge of speciesism: the species a being belongs to is not, by itself, a morally relevant difference. Equal consideration of interests means like interests count the same whoever has them. It does not mean identical treatment, because beings can have different interests.

Singer grounds moral standing in sentience, the capacity to suffer and enjoy. A being with no capacity for experience has no interests to consider. A being that can suffer does, whatever its species, intelligence or language.

Cohen rejects animal rights and Singer’s equal weighting of comparable human and animal interests. Rights are claims held within a moral community of beings who can exercise free moral judgment and accept duties. Animals cannot, so they have no rights, though Cohen grants that we may not inflict needless suffering on them.

Singer uses the argument from marginal cases to challenge capacity-based exclusions, and critics turn the same argument on Cohen. If moral standing depends on capacities such as reason or moral judgment, infants and some severely cognitively impaired humans seem to fall short. Cohen replies that standing goes with the kind of being, not the individual’s capacities. Whether that reply is principled or merely convenient is the main test of his view.

To evaluate a reply to Cohen, state what it targets, which premise of his argument it denies or which step it breaks, and what Cohen can say back. Candidates: the argument from marginal cases, and Regan’s claim that being the subject of a life is enough for rights.

The capacity to experience suffering and enjoyment. Singer takes it as the boundary of moral standing.
In Cohen, the human community within which rights and duties arise. Membership rests on belonging to a kind capable of moral judgment, not on each individual’s ability to exercise it.
A being capable of moral judgment who can be held responsible for what it does.
A being whose interests matter morally and to whom duties can be owed, whether or not it can act as a moral agent.

The objection that any capacity offered as the basis of rights, such as reason or moral judgment, is missing in some humans such as infants. Either those humans lose standing or the capacity is the wrong test.
Tom Regan’s criterion for rights: a being with beliefs, desires, memory and a welfare that matters to it, whatever its species.

study.overview: This session asked whether the species a being belongs to changes how much its suffering matters. Peter Singer says it does not: what counts is the capacity to suffer. Carl Cohen says rights belong only to members of a moral community, and animals are not members, though he still grants that needless suffering is wrong. The two authors part on the basis of moral standing, and on what that standing implies. Your task after the session is to state each argument accurately and to test one reply to Cohen by naming the premise it targets.

points.heading: Singer: equal consideration and the charge of speciesism
points.explanation: Singer starts from equal consideration of interests: like interests count the same whoever has them. He grounds moral standing in sentience, the capacity to suffer and enjoy. A being with no capacity for experience has no interests to consider. A being that can suffer does, whatever its species, intelligence or language. Preferring your own species where there is no relevant difference is speciesism, which Singer compares to racism and sexism. Equal consideration is not identical treatment, because beings can have different interests. A dog has no interest in voting, so it is not wronged by being denied the vote. Example: take the drug trial that could save many human lives but causes severe pain to twenty primates. Singer counts the primates’ suffering equally with comparable human suffering. He does not ignore the human lives, and he does not say the primates must be treated as humans are. Check the text of “All Animals Are Equal” for how he states the principle.

points.heading: Cohen: rights and the moral community
points.explanation: Cohen rejects animal rights. His argument runs in steps. Rights are claims that only members of a moral community can hold and press. Members of that community can make free moral judgments and accept duties. Animals cannot do this, so they are not members. So animals have no rights, and research on them violates none. Cohen denies that favoring humans is a prejudice. He also does not say that animal pain does not matter. He grants that needless suffering is wrong. That is a separate claim about our duties concerning suffering. It is not a premise supporting his conclusion that animals have no rights. Example: in the drug trial, Cohen finds no right of the primates violated, provided needless suffering is avoided. He answers the objection about infants and severely impaired humans with a further step: they belong because they are of a kind whose normal members can exercise moral judgment. Check this in “The Case for the Use of Animals in Biomedical Research”.

points.heading: The argument from marginal cases and Cohen’s reply
points.explanation: Singer uses the argument from marginal cases against capacity-based exclusions, and critics turn the same argument on Cohen. If moral standing depends on a capacity such as moral judgment, infants and some severely cognitively impaired humans seem to fall short. So either they lose standing, or the capacity test is wrong. Cohen replies that standing goes with the kind of being, not the individual’s capacities. Whether this reply is principled or merely convenient is the main test of his view. Cohen can say that kind membership is not arbitrary, because the human kind has the capacity at the core of rights. A strong evaluation asks whether that explains why an individual who lacks the capacity has rights. It can also ask why the human kind is the relevant kind and not the kind of creature that can suffer. Example: an infant cannot yet make moral judgments. If standing follows the kind, the infant has rights. Then ask whether a chimpanzee, which also cannot judge morally, is excluded only because of its kind.

points.heading: How to evaluate a reply to Cohen
points.explanation: A good evaluation has three parts. State what the reply targets. Say which premise of Cohen’s argument it denies or which step it breaks. Then say what Cohen can say back. Take Regan’s view that being the subject of a life is enough for rights. It targets the premise that rights require membership in a moral community of moral agents. If rights need no moral agency, the step from “animals cannot accept duties” to “animals have no rights” fails. Cohen can answer that rights are claims pressed within a community, so a being that cannot press or answer claims cannot hold them. Then press on costs: if the reply works, which humans or animals gain or lose standing? Use this template when you prepare your seminar questions and your paper on an applied question.
