segments.title: A diagnostic AI misses a tumor
segments.description:
A slide describes a hypothetical case. A hospital’s diagnostic system, trained by machine learning, misses a tumor in a way its developers cannot explain.
Students vote by show of hands on who is answerable: the developer, the hospital, the doctor, the AI itself, or no one.
The instructor asks a few students for a one-line reason, then names the question of the lecture: who is answerable when no human chose the harmful act?
segments.teacherNotes: Expect a split, with many choosing the developer. Do not resolve it. Return to this vote at the end of the Matthias segment and ask whether anyone would now change their answer. Keep the case clearly hypothetical.

segments.title: Matthias: the responsibility gap
segments.description:
Set out Matthias’s argument as numbered steps on slides.
Traditionally we ascribe responsibility to someone who had control over an action and knowledge of what it would be.
A learning automaton acts on rules it generated itself, so its manufacturer and operator can lack both.
Contrast a machine whose relevant behavior follows predictable, fixed rules with a learning system whose rules develop through experience. Matthias concludes that society must accept the gap or stop using such machines.
In pairs, students state the gap in one sentence, then return to the opening vote.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: treating the gap as ‘we cannot find the culprit’ or as a machine behaving maliciously. Matthias means the conditions for responsibility are met by no one. Stress that his claim concerns learning automata, not all software. Link control and knowledge to the reading’s own wording.

segments.title: Sparrow: killer robots and just war theory
segments.description:
Introduce Sparrow’s starting point: just war theory requires that someone can be held responsible for deaths caused in war.
Show his three candidates on a slide: the programmer, the commander and the machine. Explain why each fails once a weapon has substantial autonomy.
Draw the line Sparrow draws between limited autonomy, as in a remotely piloted drone, and substantial autonomy, where the weapon chooses targets in ways no human foresees.
State his conclusion and the respect owed to enemy combatants as persons.
segments.teacherNotes: Key misconception: Sparrow does not argue against all autonomous weapons. His problem arises only where autonomy is substantial enough that blaming a human is unfair. Sparrow argues that meaningful punishment requires genuine suffering, which the weapon systems he considers lack. Keep this scope clear: the next segment depends on it.

segments.title: Rebuild Sparrow’s argument
segments.description:
In groups of three, students receive six statements from Sparrow’s argument, shuffled, on a slide or handout.
They put the statements in order and mark which ones apply only to weapons with substantial autonomy.
Each group names the statement a defender of autonomous weapons would deny first.
Groups compare their orders on the screen.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answer key, in order:
1. Just war theory requires that someone can be held responsible for each death caused in war.
2. If a weapon’s nature makes it typically impossible to hold anyone responsible for the deaths it causes, using it in war is unjust.
3. A weapon with limited autonomy, such as a remotely piloted drone, stays under human control, so its operator or commander remains responsible.
4. A weapon with substantial autonomy chooses targets and acts in ways its programmers and commanders cannot foresee or control.
5. For such a weapon it is unfair to blame the programmer or commander, and the machine cannot be punished in a meaningful way, so no one is responsible.
6. Therefore it is unethical to deploy weapons with substantial autonomy.
Statements 4 to 6 concern substantial autonomy only; statement 3 sets the limit. Common mistake: calling all autonomous weapons unpredictable, which makes the conclusion a ban on all of them.

segments.title: Assign responsibility in one case: the Sentinel drone
segments.description:
A slide shows one hypothetical incident. An autonomous checkpoint drone, Sentinel, fires on a car carrying civilians.
Four cards give cumulative facts about this single incident. They are not alternative versions.
Display all four cards on the slide. In groups of four, assign each student one card to summarize. The group then assesses the whole case: who is responsible, and is there a responsibility gap in Matthias’s sense?
Each group reports a verdict with one reason. The instructor then changes three facts: the documentation gives no warning, the drone passed the ministry’s crowded-area testing, and the commander deploys it as approved. The instructor asks whether the verdict changes.
segments.teacherNotes:
Cards, with expected readings:
A, manufacturer: Sentinel’s targeting is learned; its engineers could not predict individual outputs. Its documentation warned it was untested in crowded areas. Risk disclosure alone does not settle the manufacturer’s responsibility; students should identify what further facts about design, testing and sale they need.
B, commander: she read the warning and deployed Sentinel at a market-side checkpoint because of a staff shortage. She knew the risk and chose to deploy: strongest candidate.
C, system: it classified the car as hostile and fired within seconds; no human could intervene. This shows the loss of real-time control, but not a gap alone.
D, ministry: it approved the purchase and waived crowded-area testing. Shares responsibility for the risk.
Expected verdict: no gap here, because B and D knowingly took the risk. In the variant, everyone acted reasonably on what they knew and nobody could foresee this harm, so a gap in Matthias’s sense plausibly opens. Some students will say the manufacturer still answers for selling a learning system at all; keep that for the seminar’s first question. Common mistake: letting one card alone decide the case.

segments.title: Leaders open: is the responsibility gap real?
segments.description:
The instructor names the two student leaders, who recall the questions they prepared.
The first leader asks whether Matthias’s gap is real, or whether the people who deploy a learning system always answer for the risk they took.
The leader draws on the Sentinel case and on Matthias’s conditions of control and knowledge.
The instructor speaks only to ask what the text requires for a gap to open.
segments.teacherNotes: Seminar, no slides. If the discussion stalls, use this fallback question: is a gap different from the unpredictability of an untrained employee or a dog? Good student moves: separate foreseeing a risk from foreseeing a specific act. Ask students to cite the reading, not paraphrase from memory.

segments.title: Leaders’ question: does any reply to Sparrow succeed?
segments.description:
The second leader asks whether Sparrow’s argument justifies refusing weapons with substantial autonomy, or whether a reply defeats it.
Students propose replies. For each, they say which premise it denies and what Sparrow can say back.
The leader keeps the discussion on the strongest reply, not the most numerous.
segments.teacherNotes:
Candidate replies if needed:
1. A commander who deploys such a weapon accepts the risk and so answers for what follows. Targets premise 5. Sparrow can say this is unfair for a killing she did not choose.
2. The state or army, not an individual, bears responsibility. Targets premise 5 by proposing an additional bearer of responsibility. Sparrow can ask who is then punished or blamed.
3. Human soldiers are also unpredictable. Targets the inference in premise 5. Sparrow can say humans can be held to account, machines cannot.

segments.title: Where do we stand? And the paper
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, whether Sparrow’s argument succeeds against weapons of substantial autonomy and which reply to it they find strongest.
The instructor links the habit of stating an objection and a reply to the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%).
Students say which applied question they have chosen for the paper, which is due next week.

keyIdeas: Matthias argues that we normally hold someone responsible only if they had control over an action and knew what it would be. A learning automaton, such as a neural network, acts on rules it develops itself. Its manufacturer and operator can lack both control and knowledge. When that happens, a responsibility gap opens.

A responsibility gap means that no one is responsible. It does not mean that one party is excused while another is still answerable. Whether a gap exists in a case depends on all the facts: who had control, who knew the risk, and who chose to deploy.

Sparrow argues from just war theory. Someone must be answerable for each killing in war. With weapons of substantial autonomy, the programmer, the commander and the machine each fail as a bearer of responsibility. So deploying them is unethical.

Sparrow’s conclusion is limited. A weapon with limited autonomy can act without immediate human control while remaining a means for which its human users can be held responsible. To assess his argument, find the premise a reply denies and what Sparrow can say back.

vocabulary.definition: A situation in which a harm occurs but no one meets the conditions for being held responsible for it.
A machine that changes its own rules of action from experience, so that its makers and operators cannot fully predict or control what it does.
The act of judging that a particular person is answerable for an action or outcome, usually because they had control and knowledge.
Autonomy great enough that a weapon chooses targets and acts in ways its programmers and commanders cannot foresee or control. Sparrow’s problem arises here.
Autonomy that leaves a human operator or commander in control of the weapon, so responsibility stays with that person.
The part of just war theory that governs conduct within war. Sparrow reads it as requiring that someone be answerable for each death caused.
A weapon that selects and attacks targets without a human deciding on each attack.

study.overview: This lesson asked who is answerable when an autonomous system causes harm and no human chose the harmful act. You read two arguments. Matthias claims a responsibility gap can open when a learning system acts on rules it developed itself. Sparrow claims it is unethical to deploy weapons with substantial autonomy, because no one could be held responsible for the deaths they cause. This guide sets out each argument, the limits on its scope, and the habit you practiced in class: state a reply, name the premise it denies, and say what the author can answer back. That habit will help you in the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%).

points.heading: Matthias’s responsibility gap
points.explanation: Matthias starts from a traditional view: we hold someone responsible only if they had control over an action and knowledge of what it would be. A learning automaton, such as a neural network, acts on rules it generated itself through experience. So its manufacturer and operator can lack both control and knowledge. When that happens, a responsibility gap opens. A gap means that no one is responsible. It does not mean that we cannot find the culprit, and it does not mean the machine is malicious. It also does not mean one party is excused while another still answers. Matthias’s claim concerns learning systems, not all software. A machine that follows predictable, fixed rules does not open a gap in this way. Example: in the hypothetical case from class, a hospital’s diagnostic system, trained by machine learning, misses a tumor in a way its developers cannot explain. Many people first blame the developer. Matthias’s test asks a harder question: did anyone have control and knowledge of that specific miss? Matthias concludes that society must accept the gap or stop using such machines. When you cite him, tie your wording to his two conditions, control and knowledge.

points.heading: Sparrow’s argument against autonomous weapons
points.explanation: Sparrow begins with just war theory, which requires that someone can be held responsible for each death caused in war. He then considers three candidates: the programmer, the commander and the machine. Suppose a weapon has substantial autonomy: it chooses targets and acts in ways its programmers and commanders cannot foresee or control. Then blaming the programmer or commander is unfair, and the machine cannot be punished in a meaningful way, because meaningful punishment requires genuine suffering, which the systems he considers lack. So no one is responsible, and deploying such weapons is unethical. He also appeals to the respect owed to enemy combatants as persons. The argument can be set out in steps: (1) someone must be answerable for each death in war; (2) a weapon that makes this typically impossible is unjust to use; (3) a limited-autonomy weapon stays under human control; (4) a substantial-autonomy weapon acts beyond human foresight and control; (5) so no one is responsible for its killings; (6) therefore deploying it is unethical.

points.heading: The limit of Sparrow’s conclusion
points.explanation: Sparrow does not argue against all autonomous weapons. His line falls between limited and substantial autonomy. A remotely piloted drone has limited autonomy. It acts without immediate human control in some respects but remains a means for which its human users can be held responsible. His problem arises only where autonomy is substantial enough that blaming a human is unfair. A common mistake is to call all autonomous weapons unpredictable. That turns his conclusion into a ban on all of them, which he does not defend. Premises 4 to 6 concern substantial autonomy only, and premise 3 sets the limit. When you write about his argument, state this scope first.

The commander read the warning and deployed it at a market-side checkpoint because of a staff shortage. The system classified the car as hostile and fired within seconds, so no human could intervene. The ministry approved the purchase and waived crowded-area testing. No single card decides the case. The loss of real-time control alone does not make a gap. Here the commander and the ministry knowingly took the risk, so there is no gap. Now change the facts: there is no warning, the drone passed crowded-area testing, and the commander deployed it as approved. Everyone acted reasonably on what they knew and nobody could foresee this harm, so a gap plausibly opens. To assess Sparrow, find the premise a reply denies and what he can say back. Reply 1: a commander who deploys the weapon accepts the risk and answers for what follows. This targets premise 5. Sparrow can say it is unfair to blame her for a killing she did not choose. Reply 2: the state or army bears responsibility. This adds another bearer. Sparrow can ask who is then punished or blamed. Reply 3: human soldiers are also unpredictable. Name the graded component this prepares: the argumentative paper on an applied question (25%), due at the end of this week.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: announcing a topic or surveying Singer and Cohen without choosing. Remind students the Sentinel case is hypothetical, so a thesis about it is conditional on the facts assumed.

segments.title: Sharpen four draft theses
segments.description:
In pairs, students decide for each of four drafts on the slide whether it is a thesis.
Where it is not, they rewrite it so it takes a side and gives a reason.
Take each draft in turn and let two or three pairs compare rewrites.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and expected answers:
1. “Animal ethics is a complicated topic.” Not a thesis: a topic, no side.
2. “Singer and Cohen both make some good points.” Not a thesis: hedges, nothing to deny.
3. “Autonomous weapons are bad.” Takes a side but gives no reason; add a because-clause drawn from Sparrow’s argument.
4. “In the Sentinel case there is no responsibility gap, because the commander deployed the drone at a market-side checkpoint after reading the warning that it was untested in crowded areas.” A good thesis, conditional on the facts.

segments.title: Premises, a bridge, and one objection with a reply
segments.description:
Model a defense on the slide using the animal case. Thesis: Cohen’s reply that standing goes with the kind of being does not answer the argument from marginal cases.
Show two premises, the bridge premise that connects them to the thesis, the strongest objection (Cohen’s reason for judging rights by kind: the capacity for moral judgment is not a test given to humans one by one), and a reply that names the premise or step it breaks.
Show what the opponent can say back.
segments.teacherNotes: Model: premise 1, some humans, such as infants, cannot make moral judgments. Premise 2, Cohen still grants them rights because normal members of their kind can. Bridge, a reason for granting rights to an individual must be a fact about that individual, not about other members of its kind. Objection, Cohen: the capacity is not a test given to humans one by one; rights belong to beings of a kind. Reply, then Cohen must say why the human kind is the relevant kind and not the kind of creature that can suffer; until he does, the bridge stands. Cohen can say back that moral agency is the capacity at the core of rights, so the kind defined by it is the right kind. Bridge premise: the claim linking the evidence to the conclusion. Common mistake: choosing a weak objection that is easy to beat. The reply must answer what Cohen actually says, not a neighboring claim.

segments.title: Build a defense for the Sentinel thesis
segments.description:
In pairs, students take thesis 4 from the earlier exercise and sketch a defense on a half page: two case premises, an explicit bridge premise explaining why those facts ground moral responsibility, one objection and a reply.
The objection must be the strongest one Matthias or Sparrow could press.
Pairs swap sketches with a neighboring pair and say whether the reply answers the objection.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected sketch: premises, the commander read the warning that Sentinel was untested in crowded areas, and she still deployed it at a market-side checkpoint. Bridge, a person who knowingly imposes a specific, serious risk on others answers for harm that realizes that risk, as someone who lends a car with known faulty brakes answers for the crash. Objection, Sparrow’s strongest: she chose to deploy, not to fire on this car, and it is unfair to blame her for a killing she did not choose. Reply, the killing is the very harm the warning named, so she answers for it as a realized risk, even though she did not choose it as an act. Sparrow can say back that this makes her answerable for the risk, not for the killing itself. The thesis is about this case only; it does not refute Sparrow’s general argument. Sketches are not collected.

segments.title: Revise a paragraph against the rubric
segments.description:
Put a draft paragraph on the slide. Students score it on the paper rubric using the levels A, B, C and D, criterion by criterion, then say which criterion to fix first.
In pairs they rewrite the paragraph, and two pairs read their revisions for the room to score.
Finally, name the two student leaders for the seminar. Each student brings a thesis, two premises, one objection with a reply, and one question about writing the paper; this feeds seminar participation (10%).
segments.teacherNotes:
Draft: “We should not eat meat. Animals can suffer, and factory farming causes them great suffering. Cohen says only moral agents have rights, but the argument from marginal cases shows he is wrong.”
Expected: the thesis takes a clear side but lacks a reason clause, so the thesis scores C. Premises C: suffering is a premise, but no bridge reaches rejecting meat. Objection and reply C at best: the draft misstates Cohen’s kind-based account as an individual moral-agency test, and invoking marginal cases does not answer his actual reply or establish the dietary conclusion.
Model revision: “We should not buy factory-farmed meat, because buying it pays for needless suffering. Animals can suffer, and factory farming causes them great suffering. Most of us can eat well without this meat, so that suffering serves only taste and convenience. Causing needless suffering is wrong, and Cohen himself grants this. Paying others to cause it is wrong for the same reason. One might object that a single purchase changes nothing, so no buyer is responsible. But buyers together keep the farms running, and each buyer chooses to join in paying for the harm.”

segments.title: Leaders open: a thesis worth defending, and the strongest objection
segments.description:
The instructor names the two student leaders, who recall the questions they prepared.
One asks how narrow a thesis can be before it stops mattering. The other asks whether a paper must answer the strongest objection even when doing so costs it the thesis.
Students bring cases from their own drafts or from Singer, Cohen, Matthias and Sparrow, and the instructor steps back.
segments.teacherNotes: Instructor exposition under two minutes. A narrow thesis such as “factory-farmed meat” still takes a side. A reply can concede part of an objection and narrow the thesis; ignoring it fails the rubric. Steer from “is it fair?” to “does the paragraph still work?”

segments.title: Test each other’s theses
segments.description:
In groups of three, each student states their thesis in one sentence.
The others say which side it takes, what a thoughtful opponent would say, and whether the reply answers that objection.
The instructor circulates and listens.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: the reply restates the thesis, or answers an easier objection than the one raised. Ask: which premise does your reply deny, or which step does it break? Students with no clear side revise the thesis here.

segments.title: Score a second paragraph, then where we stand
segments.description:
Hand each group of three a short draft paragraph on the Sentinel case. They score it on the paper rubric using A, B, C and D, criterion by criterion, and agree what to fix first.
Groups state their scores and reasons aloud and compare.
Then each student states aloud, in one sentence, their thesis and the objection they still have to answer.
segments.teacherNotes:
Draft: “The Sentinel case shows that Sparrow is right. A learning drone cannot be punished, and its designers could not predict its fire. So deploying it is unethical. Some say the commander is responsible, but I disagree.”
Expected: the thesis takes a clear side but lacks a reason clause, so the thesis scores C. Premises C: they suggest a gap but do not show no one is answerable, and give no bridge to “unethical”. Objection and reply D: the reply is only “I disagree”. Students with no side see the instructor in office hours.

keyIdeas: A paper starts from a case but must end in a thesis: a claim that takes a side someone could deny and gives its reason in a clause. A topic, a question or a survey of views is not a thesis.
A defense needs premises and a bridge premise. Each premise must carry the reader from the case to the conclusion, and a true claim with no bridge leaves a gap.

The objection to answer is the strongest one a thoughtful opponent would raise. Against a paper that rejects Cohen’s kind-based reply, that is Cohen’s reason for judging rights by kind. A reply says which premise it denies or which step it breaks, and what the opponent can say back.
Revision means scoring your own paragraph against the paper rubric levels (A, B, C, D) and fixing the weakest criterion first, not polishing the sentences that already work.

vocabulary.definition: The claim a paper defends: it takes a side someone could deny and gives its main reason.
The premise that connects the evidence or a general principle to the conclusion; without it, true premises still leave a gap.
The strongest point a thoughtful opponent could raise against the thesis or against one of its premises.
The answer to an objection, which denies a premise, breaks a step, or shows that the conclusion survives.
How far a thesis reaches. Narrowing it, for example to factory-farmed meat, can make it easier to defend while it still takes a side.

points.heading: A thesis takes a side and gives its reason
points.explanation: A topic, a question and a survey of views are not theses. A thesis is a claim someone could deny, with its reason in a clause. Take the Sentinel case, which is hypothetical, so any thesis about it is conditional on the facts assumed. The topic is “autonomous weapons”. The question is “is anyone answerable when Sentinel fires on the car carrying civilians?” A thesis is: “The commander who deploys it is answerable for exposing civilians to foreseeable risk, because the commander knowingly chose to deploy it despite the warning that it was untested in crowded areas.” Weak drafts fail in different ways. “Animal ethics is a complicated topic” is only a topic. “Singer and Cohen both make some good points” hedges and gives nothing to deny. “Autonomous weapons are bad” takes a side but gives no reason, so add a because-clause drawn from Sparrow’s argument. A good one is: “In the Sentinel case there is no responsibility gap, because the commander deployed the drone at a market-side checkpoint after reading the warning that it was untested in crowded areas.”

points.heading: A defense needs premises and a bridge premise
points.explanation: Each premise must carry the reader from the case to the conclusion. A true claim with no bridge leaves a gap. The bridge premise is the claim that links the evidence to the conclusion. Consider the thesis that Cohen’s reply, that standing goes with the kind of being, does not answer the argument from marginal cases. Two premises state what the argument from marginal cases claims and what Cohen’s reply says. The bridge premise explains why that reply fails to reach the argument. In the Sentinel sketch, the case premises are that the commander chose to deploy and had read the warning that it was untested in crowded areas. The bridge explains why those facts ground moral responsibility. Without that bridge, a draft such as “A learning drone cannot be punished, and its designers could not predict its fire. So deploying it is unethical” suggests a gap but never shows that no one is answerable, and never links the facts to “unethical”.

points.heading: Answer the strongest objection, and say what you deny
points.explanation: Choose the strongest objection a thoughtful opponent would raise, not one that is easy to beat. For the animal thesis, that is Cohen’s reason for his reply: the capacity for moral judgment is not a test given to humans one by one, so rights go with the kind. A reply must answer what he actually says, not a neighboring claim. It names the premise it denies or the step it breaks, and says what the opponent can answer back. For the Sentinel thesis, the strongest objection comes from Sparrow: the commander chose to deploy, not to fire on this car, and it is unfair to blame her for a killing she did not choose. A reply is that the killing is the very harm the warning named, so she answers for it as a realized risk. Sparrow can say back that this makes her answerable for the risk, not for the killing itself. Be careful with the animal draft. It treats Cohen’s view as a test of individual moral agency, but his account is kind-based, so “the argument from marginal cases shows he is wrong” does not answer him. A reply may concede part of an objection and narrow the thesis. Ignoring the objection fails the rubric. Replying only “I disagree” scores Beginning.

points.heading: Revise by fixing the weakest criterion first
points.explanation: Score your own paragraph on the paper rubric, criterion by criterion, using A, B, C and D. Then fix the weakest criterion before polishing sentences that already work. Take the draft “We should not eat meat. Animals can suffer, and factory farming causes them great suffering. Cohen says only moral agents have rights, but the argument from marginal cases shows he is wrong.” Its thesis takes a clear side but lacks a reason clause. Its premises score C: suffering is a premise, but no bridge reaches rejecting meat. Its objection and reply score C at best, because it misstates Cohen and does not reach the dietary conclusion. The revision narrows and repairs it: “We should not buy factory-farmed meat, because buying it pays for needless suffering. Animals can suffer, and factory farming causes them great suffering. Most of us can eat well without this meat, so that suffering serves only taste and convenience. Causing needless suffering is wrong, and Cohen himself grants this. Paying others to cause it is wrong for the same reason. One might object that a single purchase changes nothing, so no buyer is responsible. But buyers together keep the farms running, and each buyer chooses to join in paying for the harm.” A narrow thesis still takes a side. When you doubt a reply, ask whether the paragraph still works, rather than whether it is fair.

segments.title: Retrieval grid: test and objection
segments.description:
Show a four-row grid on a slide, with one row each for utilitarianism, Kant, virtue ethics and social contract theory.
In pairs, students recall each theory’s test for right action and its strongest objection.
The instructor reveals the grid and students correct their own notes.
segments.teacherNotes:
Expected answers, one per line:
Utilitarianism: maximize overall well-being; objection: it can justify sacrificing an innocent person, and it is very demanding.
Kant: act only on a maxim you can will as universal law; objection: prohibiting lies even to protect an innocent person, as in the murderer at the door.
Virtue ethics: do what the virtuous person would do; objection: weak guidance in dilemmas.
Contract theory: follow rules rational people would accept; objection: it leaves out those who cannot bargain, such as animals.

segments.title: One case, four theories: giving to famine relief
segments.description:
Put Singer’s case on a slide: you can give a large share of your income to famine relief at a modest cost to your own comfort.
The instructor applies each theory’s test in turn and records the verdicts in a comparison table.
Students note where the reasoning, not only the verdict, diverges.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely verdicts: utilitarian, give while an additional donation produces more overall benefit than harm; Kantian, an imperfect duty of beneficence, with latitude in how to help but a requirement to adopt others’ happiness as an end; virtue ethics, generosity is a virtue but sets no fixed amount; contract theory, weak or no duty to strangers outside the agreement. Stress that verdicts differ in strength.

segments.title: Anatomy of a structured answer
segments.description:
Show a model answer to the famine relief case in five labeled moves: thesis, test applied, strongest objection, direct reply, verdict.
The instructor shows how the same answer would be scored at the rubric levels A to D, using thesis, premises, and objection and reply as the criteria.
Students mark where each move begins.
segments.teacherNotes: Warn against the usual losses: summarizing a theory instead of applying it, a strawman objection, a reply that restates the thesis, and a verdict that does not follow from the premises.

segments.title: Plan and score exam-style outlines
segments.description:
In groups of three, students choose one exam-style question and sketch a structured answer: thesis, test applied, objection, reply, verdict.
They name one passage or example from the readings to support the central premise.
Two groups then present their outlines briefly, and the class scores each from A to D on thesis, premises, and objection and reply, and names the weakest criterion.
segments.teacherNotes:
Questions, with points a good outline makes:
1. Does utilitarianism fail because of justice? Use Mill’s reply from secondary principles; then test it against the stipulation that the framing is never discovered.
2. Can Kant’s theory handle apparent conflicts of duty? Distinguish perfect and imperfect duties, apply the distinction to a specific case, and assess whether it resolves the apparent conflict.
3. Does virtue ethics guide action? Use Aristotle’s mean and the virtuous person’s judgment.
Groups that finish early outline an applied question, such as whether Cohen’s appeal to kind answers the argument from marginal cases. Pick presenters who chose different questions. Name the two seminar leaders at the end; they prepared questions in advance.

segments.title: Leaders open: switch and footbridge
segments.description:
The instructor names the two student leaders, who recall the questions they prepared.
The first leader asks which theory best explains the difference between Thomson’s switch and footbridge cases.
Students answer by naming a theory, a premise and a passage from the readings.
segments.teacherNotes: Instructor speaks under two minutes. Expect utilitarians to struggle with the footbridge intuition, Kantians to cite treating a person merely as a means, others to cite Thomson’s rights-based view. Press for a premise, not just a verdict.

segments.title: Leaders’ question: Singer and where theories break down
segments.description:
The second leader asks whether Singer’s argument on famine depends on utilitarianism, or whether a Kantian or a contract theorist could accept his conclusion on other grounds.
Students then each pick one theory and name the objection that most threatens it.
Other students reply on the theory’s behalf and say whether the reply works.
segments.teacherNotes: Good moves: the drowning child premise is weaker than full utilitarianism; Nagel limits egalitarian socioeconomic justice to a shared sovereign state while recognizing humanitarian duties to strangers; Cohen denies animal rights but recognizes obligations concerning animals; mutual-benefit contract theory faces the objection that animals cannot bargain for protection. If talk drifts to rejecting all theories, ask what the objector would put in their place.

segments.title: Spoken exam answers in pairs
segments.description:
In pairs, students take one exam-style question from the lecture and give a two-minute spoken answer in the structure practiced there.
The listener scores it A to D on thesis, premises, and objection and reply, and names the weakest criterion.
Partners swap roles.
segments.teacherNotes: Pairs choose different questions: justice objection to utilitarianism, conflicting duties for Kant, or action guidance in virtue ethics. Circulate and listen; step in only if a pair is stuck. Nothing is collected.

segments.title: Where do we stand?
segments.description:
Each student states aloud, in one sentence, which theory they would defend on an exam question and the objection they most need to answer.
The instructor closes by naming the two or three skills to practice before the final exam.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep each statement to about twenty seconds. In a large group, ask students to answer in pairs first and call on a sample. Skills: apply the test to the case, state the strongest objection fairly, make the reply answer it directly. Remind students that the exam covers the whole course, including cultural relativism and the applied questions on Nagel, animals and responsibility for AI.

keyIdeas: Each theory supplies a test for right action: utilitarianism asks which act produces the best consequences for all affected, Kant asks whether your maxim can be willed as a universal law, virtue ethics asks what a person of good character would do, and social contract theory asks which rules rational people would agree to for mutual benefit.

Each theory has a strongest objection that a good answer states fairly: utilitarianism and justice or demandingness, Kant and apparent conflicts of duty, virtue ethics and action guidance, contract theory and those who cannot bargain.
Putting the theories on one case shows where they agree on the verdict, where they differ, and where they reach the same verdict for different reasons.
A strong exam answer is a structured argument: a thesis, the theory’s test applied to the case, the strongest objection, a direct reply, and a verdict that follows from the premises.

A case that fits a principle’s conditions but yields a verdict there is good reason to reject, used to challenge the principle.
An argument organized in set moves: thesis, test applied to the case, strongest objection, direct reply and verdict.

Put all four on one case, Singer’s famine relief example, and you can see where they agree, where they differ, and where they reach similar verdicts for different reasons.
